title: The State-Level History-Makers in the 2026 Midterms - Time Magazine
text: Listen 00:00 1.0 x 13:31 Narrated by TIME AI. Last week’s midterm elections, in which Democrats regained control of Congress , saw several victors make historic national firsts , including the first Muslim U.S. Senator-elect, the first openly gay male U.S. Senator-elect, and the first Native American female governor-elect. But a number of states also elected barrier-breakers—from their first transgender state lawmakers to their first Latino or first Black governors. Read More: Exclusive: Voters of Color Were ‘Driving Force’ Behind Midterm Rout, Say Key Strategists Advertisement Here are some of the election-winners who made history in their states. Katherine Robertson, Alabama’s first female Attorney General-elect, during a campaign event in Mobile on Oct. 2, 2026. Andi Rice—Bloomberg/Getty Images Alabama elected its first female Attorney General, Republican Katherine Robertson, who beat Democrat Jeff McLaughlin. “Thanks to every one of you who filled in the bubble with my name, a small-town girl from Selma is now the first woman elected Attorney General,” Robertson said in a statement after Election Day. “This victory is for you.” Alabama also elected its first openly transgender state lawmaker, Democratic software engineer Allison Montgomery, who flipped a seat held by Republicans in the state House of Representatives. Montgomery’s gender identity came under attack during the campaign, though she tried to keep the focus on issues such as education and affordability. Advertisement “People across the political spectrum seem to be making a big deal out of the trans thing, but that’s not why I ran for this seat,” Montgomery told the Alabama Political Reporter , saying she is tired of hearing how “historic” her victory was. “I felt a calling to be a public servant, and now I’m gonna do my best for all of us, regardless of how you voted or what you think of my gender.” Arizona elected its first Indian American to the U.S. House of Representatives and first Indigenous woman to the state’s utility commission. Democrat Amish Shah, an emergency room doctor and former state legislator, beat the GOP nominee, former NFL placekicker and broadcaster Jay Feely, to succeed retiring Republican David Schweikert as U.S. representative for Arizona’s 1st district. Meanwhile, Democrat Clara Pratte, a member of the Navajo Nation, was elected to Arizona’s Corporation Commission, the state’s five-member utility-regulation body that was previously entirely Republican but will now have two Democrats after Tuesday’s election. Pratte is reportedly Arizona’s first indigenous woman elected to statewide office. Democrat Xavier Becerra will become California’s first elected Latino governor after beating Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton in the race to succeed term-limited Democrat Gavin Newsom. Becerra will technically be the second Latino to hold the office, as Romualdo Pacheco served as governor by succession for a short time in 1875. Becerra’s mother was born in Jalisco, Mexico. She immigrated to the U.S. after marrying his father, a construction worker. Becerra first served as a U.S. Representative for California between 1993 and 2017, before his appointment as California’s first Latino Attorney General in 2017 and election to the role in 2018. He was then the first Latino Health and Human Services Secretary, serving in former President Joe Biden’s Cabinet from 2021 to 2025. “There is no American greatness without California, and there is no California without our diverse communities,” Becerra said during his victory speech Tuesday . “Diversity is not our shortcoming—it’s our superpower. And it isn’t our finish line—it’s our bottomline.” Advertisement Rep.-elect Melat Kiros during the Colorado Democrats’ Election Night watch party in Denver on Nov. 3, 2026. Aaron Ontiveroz—The Denver Post/Getty Images Democratic socialist Melat Kiros , a 29-year-old Ethiopian-born lawyer turned doctoral student, will become the first Black woman to represent Colorado in Congress, after she was elected to represent the state’s 1st district in the U.S. House. Kiros, who was born in Addis Ababa in May 1997, will also be the first Gen Z woman in Congress. Also making history in the state is Amanda Gonzalez , who was elected the first Latina and first openly LGBT Colorado Secretary of State. Advertisement Republican Rep. Byron Donalds will be Florida’s first Black governor, after he was elected to succeed Ron DeSantis. Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former school principal and the daughter of Indian immigrants, won the race to represent Florida’s 22nd district in the U.S. House and will become the state’s first South Asian congressperson. In Georgia, Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds will be the state’s first Black woman elected Secretary of State (after Robyn Crittenden was briefly appointed to the role in 2018), Democrat Tanya Miller will be the state’s first female Attorney General, and Democrat Nikki Porcher will be the state’s first Black female Commissioner of Labor. Meanwhile, Democrat Bentley Hudgins became the first trans and nonbinary person elected to Georgia’s state legislature. Advertisement Rep.-elect J.D. Ford, then a state senator, speaks at the Indiana Statehouse in Indianapolis on Dec. 11, 2025. Kaiti Sullivan—Bloomberg/Getty Images Democratic state senator J.D. Ford will be Indiana’s first openly LGBT member of Congress after beating Republican incumbent Rep. Victoria Spartz, securing a seat Democrats haven’t held since 1992. Ford, who is gay, has been a strong advocate for LGBT rights and previously made history when, in 2018, he unseated a 13-year incumbent who campaigned against same-sex marriage to become the first openly gay member of the Indiana state legislature. Democrat Josh Turek will be Iowa’s first U.S. Senator with a permanent disability, after the state lawmaker defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate election in Iowa since 2008. Advertisement The 47-year-old Turek, who will replace outgoing Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, was born with spina bifida, a birth defect that he says stemmed from his father’s exposure to Agent Orange while on deployment to Vietnam. Turek pursued wheelchair basketball in college and competed professionally in Europe. He’s competed in four Paralympic Games and won gold in two. “Iowa, we have done it—what they said was impossible,” Turek said in his victory speech Tuesday. “Together, Iowa, we have proven that the impossible was possible.” Rep.-Elect Dan Koh gives remarks alongside members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus during a new member orientation press conference outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026. Aaron Schwartz—Getty Images Democrat Dan Koh, whose father is Korean and whose mother is Lebanese, won the race to represent Massachusetts’ 6th district in Congress, beating Republican Micah Quinney Jones. Koh’s win makes him the first Asian American elected to represent the state in the U.S. House. Koh served in the Biden Administration as White House Deputy Cabinet Secretary and was previously Chief of Staff to the U.S. Department of Labor. Advertisement Several Democrats have made history in Michigan. State senator Jeremy Moss will become the state’s first openly LGBT member of Congress after he was elected to represent Michigan’s 11th district. Moss defeated Republican Ethan Baker in the race to replace Democrat Haley Stevens , who lost to Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senator. Jason Hoskins, who was elected to replace Moss in his state senate seat, will become the first openly gay Black member of the Michigan Senate. Sean McCann, another state senator, will become the first Native American elected to Congress from Michigan. The Democrat, who discovered that he belonged to the federally recognized Citizen Potawatomi Nation just this year , beat Republican incumbent Rep. Bill Huizenga to represent Michigan’s 4th district. Advertisement And lastly, clinical spiritual care provider Joanna Whaley will become Michigan’s first elected transgender legislator after winning election to the state’s lower house. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar will become Minnesota’s first female governor after she defeated Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth. Klobuchar, who will succeed Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, has broken the glass ceiling before: she was the first female Hennepin County attorney and the first woman elected to represent the state in the U.S. Senate, a seat she has held since 2007. In her victory speech, Klobuchar thanked her supporters for her milestones and celebrated other ceilings broken, including the election of the country’s first Native American female senator, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith. Democrat Denise Powell beat Republican Brinker Harding to represent Nebraska’s 2nd district. Powell, a Democratic activist who co-founded the Women Who Run Nebraska political action committee to coach local women to run for office, is Hispanic and will become the state’s first Latina elected to Congress. Advertisement “We made history tonight,” Powell said in her victory speech Tuesday . “Not only did you help elect the first woman and first Latina to ever hold this seat, but you helped send a clear message to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue,” she said, referring to the Trump White House. Teresa Benitez-Thompson is the first Latina elected to the U.S. House from Nevada. The Democratic former state assembly majority leader defeated Republican David Flippo, flipping the state’s 2nd district that’s been held by Republicans since its creation in the 1980s. Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford will also make history as the state’s first Black governor, after he defeated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. He will join other historic Black governors-elect, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Byron Donalds in Florida. Nevada Gov.-elect Aaron D. Ford at the Nevada Democratic Party’s election watch party in Las Vegas on Nov. 3, 2026. Ethan Miller—Getty Images Advertisement Tya Mathis-Coleman, Nevada’s treasurer-elect, will also become the state’s first Black woman elected to statewide constitutional office. Egyptian American surgeon Adam Hamawy will become New Jersey’s first Muslim representative in Congress after the Democrat beat Republican Gregg Mele in the contest to represent the state’s 12th district. Hamawy, a former U.S. Army combat surgeon, will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman. Hamawy volunteered for medical missions in the Gaza Strip in 2024 and 2025 and spoke throughout his campaign about what he witnessed there. In his victory speech , he alluded to Islamophobia in the U.S., saying, “I have never seen anti-Muslim hate as open and as loud and as accepted as it is today.” Advertisement Democratic socialists won big in New York —and several made history, too. Claire Valdez, a New York assemblymember backed by popular New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , will head to Capitol Hill in January as the state's first Native American woman in Congress, after her election to represent the state’s 7th district. Valdez, a Latina and a citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation, bested Republican Melvin Rivera in a race to succeed retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez. Darializa Avila Chevalier, a community organizer who worked for Mamdani’s mayoral campaign, will be the first Muslim to represent New York in Congress, after she defeated Republican Jomo Williams to succeed Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom Avila Chevalier beat in the Democratic primary, as representative of the state’s 13th district. Another member of the Democratic Socialists of America, state senator-elect Aber Kawas, will become the first Palestinian American in the New York State Legislature. Kawas acknowledged the feat on social media, posting : “We made history.” Advertisement Meanwhile, social worker Illapa Sairitupac and attorney David Siffert jointly set a milestone in the State Assembly after they were elected as New York’s first two openly nonbinary state lawmakers. Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton greets supporters at an Election Night watch party in Columbus on Nov. 3, 2026. Jeff Swensen—Getty Images Dr. Amy Acton , a Democrat who previously served as the director of Ohio’s health department at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, defeated Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the race to become Ohio’s next governor. While Nancy Hollister served as Ohio’s first female governor for 11 days from 1998 to 1999, Hollister assumed the post through succession after Gov. George Voinovich resigned following his election to the U.S. Senate. Acton, therefore, is the first woman Ohio elected to be governor. Advertisement Democrat Kim Ahern, a former state prosecutor, defeated Republican Alan Gordon in the race to become Rhode Island’s next Attorney General. Ahern pointed to the historic nature of her success, including becoming the state’s first openly LGBT Attorney General and first Democratic woman in the role: “I am especially proud we made history tonight. It was the first time in our state’s history women will hold a majority of our general offices. I am honored to be part of that milestone,” she said in her victory speech. Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn was elected Tennessee’s first female governor , beating Democratic candidate Jerri Green and several independents. When she takes office next year, Blackburn, who will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Bill Lee, will also become Tennessee’s oldest governor at 74, taking the record from Republican Alfred Alexander Taylor, who was 72 when he took office in 1921. Advertisement Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa speaks at her Election Night watch party in Austin on Nov. 3, 2026. Mikala Compton—The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images Democrat Gina Hinojosa was elected as the new governor of Texas, becoming the first Hispanic person elected to the office in the state's history. Hinojosa is the first Democrat elected to the state’s governor’s mansion in more than three decades. “I can’t help but think of my grandmother who used to tell me, ‘ No te dejes .’ ‘Know your worth, and fight for it,’” Hinojosa said in her victory speech . “A lot of Latinas in Texas grew up hearing those same words from their own mothers and abuelas. This year, we lived them, and we changed this state.” Advertisement Jaelynn Scott, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, will be the first openly transgender person to serve in Washington's Legislature. Scott, the executive director of the Lavender Rights Project, a Black trans advocacy organization, told nonprofit newsroom The 19th on Tuesday that her win felt “pretty surreal.” “The fact is, people that look like me and have my identity in 2026 are used to being under attack — not leading,” she said. “I think it was because of what’s happening to us, and really maybe even a bit of fear about what might happen to me and my community, that inspired me to run. I never thought we would get this far.” Democrat David Crowley was elected Wisconsin’s first Black governor, after defeating Republican Tom Tiffany in the race to replace Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, who chose not to run for reelection. Advertisement Other Democratic candidates also made history in Wisconsin. JoCasta Zamarripa became the first Latina elected to statewide office as Wisconsin’s Secretary of State. Yee Leng Xiong, who was elected as state treasurer, will become Wisconsin’s first Hmong statewide elected official. And Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, a former food-service worker who beat Republican Nina Chat in a race to represent the state assembly’s 76th district, will become the first transgender woman in the Wisconsin state legislature. “I think about when I was a kid, had I seen people that were trans doing things like being in government and being on television and living life,” Martinez-Rutherford, 56, told the Capital Times . “I hope that it gives kids or families of trans people hope that they can live to be adults and that their children are going to be safe because they have somebody representing them.”

title: City of Madison to honor road traffic victims - WKOW
text: MADISON, Wis. (WKOW) — The City of Madison's Vision Zero initiative will recognize the World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims during the week of remembrance, Nov. 9-15. Madison will join many communities around the world in honoring those who have lost their lives or been seriously injured in traffic crashes and standing in solidarity with the families, friends and loved ones left behind. As part of this observance, Vision Zero Madison will install a public display to remember lives lost on roadways, raise awareness about the devastating impacts of traffic crashes and encourage the community to reflect on the shared responsibility everyone has to make streets safer. "In Madison, we get to school and work by walking, biking, bussing, or driving. Our streets need to be safe for everyone," Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said. Slowing down, yielding to pedestrians, avoiding distractions, driving sober, wearing seat belts and looking out for vulnerable road users are actions everyone can take to save lives. The city is prioritizing smarter street design and transportation systems, in addition to education and enforcement. The city encourages residents to take time during the week of remembrance to view the display, honor those affected by traffic violence and consider the ways individual choices and community action can help prevent future tragedies. The display will be located at Burr Jones Park at 1820 East Washington Avenue along the mixed-use path by East Washington Avenue from Nov. 9-15. Vision Zero Madison is the City of Madison's commitment to eliminating traffic fatalities and serious injuries. The initiative recognizes that human mistakes are inevitable, but traffic deaths and life-altering injuries should not be. "Through Vision Zero Madison, we are working toward a future where no one has to experience the devastating loss of a loved one because of a traffic crash. One life lost is too many, and we all have a role to play in making Vision Zero a reality," Rhodes-Conway said.

title: Downriver Democrat Joanna Whaley Makes History as Michigan's First Trans Lawmaker - Hoodline
text: Michigan State Capitol — Legislature Where Whaley Will Serve Google Street View Voters in Michigan's 2nd House District elected Joanna Whaley to represent them, making her the first openly transgender woman ever elected to Michigan's state legislature. The Downriver district covers Allen Park, Lincoln Park, Melvindale and part of Southgate, and Whaley's win there is already being counted among the most historic results of the 2026 midterms. Whaley defeated Republican Ron Kokinda in the race for state representative, according to The News-Herald , which reported she took 22,343 votes to Kokinda's 13,414 — a tally the outlet calculated as 62 percent of votes cast. Other outlets reported different vote-share figures for the same race: The 19th put her total at 63 percent, FOX 2 Detroit reported 62 percent, and Pride Source reported 62.5 percent while noting as of November 6 that results remained unofficial. Whatever the precise number, every account agrees Whaley's win was decisive. As reported by CBS News Detroit , voters chose Whaley to represent the district, cementing her place in Michigan political history. She had already cleared a major hurdle in August, winning the Democratic primary for District 2 on August 4, according to the Detroit Free Press . Whaley's campaign centered on pocketbook issues rather than her historic candidacy. As Michigan Advance reported, her run was not focused on her transgender identity but on affordability and accountability for her Downriver district. The News-Herald reported that her priorities include halting utility rate increases, working toward a single-payer health care system and bringing down medical costs in the meantime. Whaley brings an unusual background to the statehouse. The 19th described her as a hospital chaplain and a former megachurch pastor, details that paint a picture of a candidate whose path to office ran through pastoral and spiritual care work rather than traditional political channels. The road to victory wasn't without danger. A photo caption published by the Detroit Free Press on October 16 noted that Whaley had endured several threats requiring a security detail, a detail that underscores the pressures facing the state's first openly transgender legislator even before she took office. Whaley's win was one of several LGBTQ+ milestones in Michigan's 2026 midterms. Michigan Advance reported that nine openly LGBTQ+ people were set to serve as Michigan state legislators following the election, and Pride Source separately reported that nine out LGBTQ+ legislative candidates won seats statewide. Michigan Advance also reported that Jeremy Moss was elected to Michigan's 11th Congressional District, becoming the state's first openly gay member of Congress, and that Jason Hoskins became the first openly gay Black member of the Michigan Senate. The trend extended beyond Michigan's borders. A report from Gayety said trans candidates also topped unofficial statehouse returns in Wisconsin and Alabama, with Madison City Council member Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford leading in Wisconsin's 76th Assembly District and Allison Montgomery leading in Alabama's House District 25. Nationally, the picture is more mixed. The LGBTQ+ Victory Institute's 2026 report counted 1,359 known out LGBTQ+ elected officials across the country as of May 30, before the midterms — and found that while the number of transgender men in elected office rose 22.2 percent, the number of transgender women stayed the same over the same period, making Whaley's Downriver victory a notable exception within that broader data. title: As Rhodes-Conway prepares to leave office, the Capital Improvement Plan could become her lasting legacy - The Daily Cardinal
text: Mayor of Madison Satya Rhodes-Conway speaks at the construction site of the future Metro Transit Satellite Bus Facility on Madison’s east side, on March 6, 2024. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway renounced her reelection bid after developing the 2027 Executive Capital Budget, a part of the five-year Capitol Improvement plan which highlights investment in police body-worn cameras and affordable housing. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would seek her third term on July 16. Just a week later, Madison Police Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson shot and killed Cory Ruiz ,  sparking large, citywide protests. Two weeks after the initial shooting, Rhodes-Conway made the controversial decision to remove an encampment in Ruiz’s honor. The city’s subsequent responses to the event drew criticism from all sides, including a 12-hour Common Council meeting that terminated the Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeriamique Glass.  Rhodes-Conway then said she and other public officials had faced threats and misogynistic harassment, and announced she would not run for reelection. “She is calling attention to a problem that is not new, but it is increasing,” District 8 Alder Ellen Zhang said in an email to The Daily Cardinal.  The announcement comes in the middle of her 2027 Executive Capital Budget awaiting approval.  The backlash from the Ruiz shooting prompted the Madison Community Foundation (MCF) to grant $350,000 to the city to fund police body-worn cameras. The grant gave way for body cameras to roll out on a one-year timeline rather than the initial three-year plan.  “I think it's time to take a step forward on this long-debated equipment decision, which is why I included funding for this technology in this year's capital budget,” Rhodes-Conway wrote in the budget release.  The 2027 Executive Capital Budget includes $400,000 for equipment related to body-worn cameras, according to City Communications Manager Dylan Brogan. He told the Cardinal he hopes half of that funding will be covered through a federal grant the city is applying for.  Funding for body-worn cameras has previously been shot down by alders over cost concerns. Brogan said he believes the 2027 budget will pass after review and amendments from the council. Zhang also said it is likely for the Madison Police Department to start using body cameras after the grant received from MCF.  The Common Council will begin budget deliberations on Nov. 10.  Next year’s budget will jump-start the body-cam program for years to come, Brogan said. The investment will cover operating costs for implementing the program and staff needed. He said if the budget passes, every police officer will be equipped with body-worn cameras by the end of 2027.  Moving forward, Brogan said maintaining the program will be up to a future council for the 2028 budget. This would include operating expenses for record-keeping and managing software. The 2027 budget also includes plans for affordable housing investment, with the goal of creating 15,000 more homes by 2030. “Like many in our community, I'm deeply frustrated by the affordability crisis and the associated costs of mitigating the problem instead of solving it,” Rhodes-Conway said in her plan.  Brogan noted investment through the Community Development Authority will not be affected in the near future. He said the city will continue to invest in affordable housing through the Affordable Housing Fund and other programs in the 2027 budget.  Zhang thanked Rhodes-Conway for her service to the community.  “I have appreciated her guidance and patience to explain the unfamiliar scope of city government, and I admire how she remains calm and focused during intense situations,” she told the Cardinal.  Zhang pointed to the Bus Rapid Transit System, affordable housing programs and State Street placemaking as some projects enabled by the mayor that benefit University of Wisconsin-Madison students. title: Madison’s mayoral race adds a candidate: Who's announced so far? - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Jason Ilstrup, president of Downtown Madison Inc., announced his bid for mayor Tuesday, joining the pool of candidates seeking to replace current Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. Rhodes-Conway decided she will not seek reelection to a third term next year, citing “concerns about the toll of serving in public office.” Ilstrup announced his campaign Tuesday morning at the Neighborhood House Community Center, where he served on the board for more than a decade. Ilstrup has a long history in Madison’s business community, starting as a bellman at the Madison Concourse Hotel, opening HotelRed, and now leading Downtown Madison Inc. His platform includes changing city policies such as zoning to address housing affordability; cutting regulatory steps and fees to help people start small businesses; and improving the city's responsiveness to residents. So far, the Cap Times has confirmed that in addition to Ilstrup, the list of candidates includes: former City Council members Brian Benford and Syed Abbas; former Dane County Board member April Kigeya; One City Schools CEO and founder Kaleem Caire ; athletic trainer and Monkey Bar Gym owner Jon Hinds; hospitality and food service director Larry Williams; and former Golden Gloves boxer and east side bartender Marcus Johnson. Candidates for spring elections have until early Jan. 5 to file their final paperwork before the primary on Feb. 16. The two candidates with the most votes will advance to the April 6 ballot. Former Dane County Board member April Kigeya is one of eight people running to be Madison's mayor next spring. Former Dane County Board member April Kigeya announced her bid to be Madison’s mayor in September. Kigeya is running her platform on challenging Madison’s reputation as a city with affordable housing, good-paying jobs, and a responsive city government. As mayor, she said, she hopes to prioritize reforming city government so it “listens, responds and delivers for working people.” “The challenges facing our city are real. But so is our ability to solve them,” she said in a press release. “When we listen to one another, bring people together, and put working families at the center of our decisions, we can build One Madison, where all of us belong and all of us can thrive.” Benford, also a former north side representative, spoke with the Cap Times about why he’s getting back into local politics after stepping back in 2023 to make space for younger leaders. In an interview, he said the lack of leadership following the Madison police shooting of Corey Ruiz on July 22 has inspired him to throw his hat into the ring and run a campaign fueled by the “people’s power.” Brian Benford stepped back after two terms on the Madison City Council but said he felt called to action after the death of Corey Ruiz. Benford has decades of experience as a social worker and, more recently, as a success coach for UW-Madison’s Odyssey Project. He described himself as a nontraditional politician and is running his campaign on social justice, racial equity and transparency. Abbas, a former City Council president, announced his candidacy in late August. Abbas works as the deputy legislative director for the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. His platform priorities include housing, fiscal responsibility, social and environmental justice, and transportation. The former City Council president said he wants to increase pathways to own homes and condos, reduce property taxes and expand regional transit. Caire announced his campaign in late September and told the Cap Times he’s been thinking about running since the 1990s. Caire is running on a platform of bringing independent politics and leadership experience, finding solutions to local problems, diversifying the city government workforce, strategizing with regional partners and expanding homeownership opportunities. The mayoral candidate and CEO of One City Schools said he will run a community-driven campaign rather than one shaped by a few endorsers. The Cap Times will provide more information about the remaining candidates in the coming weeks. Voters will cast ballots next spring for a leader responsible for a local government corps of about 3,000 workers who serve about 300,000 people. Mayoral terms are four years, and there are no term limits for the position. The mayor’s role is essentially to act as the city’s chief executive officer, responsible for recommending policy to the City Council, breaking tie votes and vetoing legislation. The mayor also fulfills an executive role by ensuring municipal laws are enforced and that city officers and employees do their jobs. The mayor also appoints the city’s department leaders and some committee members, and chooses deputy mayors who act as liaisons for the agencies. Half of the council will be up for election again in April — the odd-numbered districts — in addition to the mayor. A primary election will be held in February, and the two candidates with the most votes in each race will advance to the April general election. Aside from police accountability and racial disparities in Madison, voters will likely weigh several other persistent issues in the spring election. Among them are affordable housing, public safety, community input, transparency, municipal spending and social justice. title: Madison approves 2027 budget with funding for new body camera program - WKOW
text: MADISON (WKOW) -- The Madison Common Council has approved a capital and operating budget for 2027 that maintains essential services while keeping property taxes stable. The budget prioritizes community safety and key services while building on recent progress to create more homes and keep the city affordable, according to a press release. Despite continued state-imposed restrictions, the city avoided cuts to important services by finding efficiencies and ways to maximize impact. "This year's budget sets Madison up for future success with investments in our infrastructure that are essential to our high quality of life," Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said. "Though difficult, we avoided cuts to important services by finding efficiencies and ways to maximize our impact." The budget includes nearly a million dollars in efficiencies to limit the burden on property taxpayers while preserving essential city services. It adds $12 million for the affordable housing fund to help meet the city's goal of creating 15,000 more homes by 2030. The city has added 2,534 net homes so far in 2026 and is on pace for its strongest year since before the pandemic. The budget continues investment in social housing through the Triangle Redevelopment Project. Other key investments include violence prevention programs and a new body-worn camera program. The budget funds a 10th ambulance company and staffing at the recently opened Imagination Center Library. "We were able to avoid new special charges that were called for in the five-year operating budget plan, as well as reductions in service that would disproportionately impact the residents who can least afford it," Rhodes-Conway said. For the first time, the 2027 operating budget includes agency data from Results Madison . The initiative aims to make it easier for the public, city staff and elected officials to make data-informed policy decisions.

title: Meet the Madison comedian who will become Wisconsin’s first transgender legislator - WPR
text: For much of her life, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford did not envision herself entering politics. She chuckles when she remembers a high school trip she took to Washington D.C. “I was like, “Let’s go to Georgetown and shop,”‘ the Madison alder recalled in an interview with WPR. “The older I got, and … especially after I transitioned, I realized how impactful politics are on our daily lives.” WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. When she’s sworn in early next year, Martinez-Rutherford, a Democrat, will become the first transgender member of Wisconsin’s state Legislature. That’s after winning more than 92 percent of the vote in Wisconsin’s 76th Assembly District, a deep-blue district that includes Madison and Maple Bluff. It’s a milestone she takes seriously. “I think it makes a huge difference for kids to see themselves represented and represented in media and politics and whatever field they want to go in,” Martinez-Rutherford said. “And we are everywhere.” Martinez-Rutherford grew up in Celina, Texas, as part of what she describes as a “highly religious” Christian family. She was an artsy theater kid, and she used to get called “sissy.” “I take that as a compliment now,” she said. “So, yeah, I did not fit in.” As an adult, Martinez-Rutherford moved around a lot, including to Indianapolis, New York and Los Angeles. She worked — briefly — as a pastor and has also been been a flight attendant, actor and stand-up comedian. More than a decade ago, two of her best friends convinced her to move to Madison, where she took what started as a summer job at Monty’s Blue Plate Diner. One of her co-workers there was trans. “I was like, ‘Holy cow! In the middle of the country, there’s another trans person just living their daily lives,”‘ she remembered. “It was very exciting, and I got to meet a lot of people who are still friends of mine.” Martinez-Rutherford, who is now 56, transitioned to female when she was in her 30s. In January, when she makes history as Wisconsin’s first transgender legislator, she will also mark the 20th anniversary of her transition. “Here we are in the weirdest turn of events, a fat trans lady who is a comedian is now going to be representative,” she said. “It’s bizarre and exciting and terrifying and cool.” Along with her creative pursuits in comedy, Martinez-Rutherford has spent years in the food service industry. That includes waiting tables, bartending and working for a friend’s food truck. She says she knows what it’s like to go without health insurance. And she says housing insecurity has forced her to couch-surf while relying on the generosity of friends. “I’ve experienced homelessness in the sense that I was doubled up,” she said. “I, fortunately, was never unsheltered, but there are so many people that have no other option.” During the COVID-19 pandemic, Martinez-Rutherford says she was inspired by fundraisers and mutual aid efforts to help people who were struggling. She became the first transgender woman elected to Madison’s Common Council in 2023. She filed to run for that council seat again in an April 2025 election, but announced she would drop out of the race that January, citing personal and medical reasons. Although she endorsed her opponent, it was too late for Martinez-Rutherford to be removed from the ballot, and she won anyway. She decided to assume the role representing part the city’s east side. Martinez-Rutherford launched her bid for the state Assembly, after state Rep. Francesca Hong announced her bid for governor, and declined to seek reelection to that seat. Hong, a Democratic socialist, narrowly lost in the Democratic primary to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who is now the governor-elect. During a five-way Democratic primary in August 2026, Martinez-Rutherford took close to 30 percent of the vote, beating the second-place candidate, former Madison Alder Juliana Bennett, by about 500 votes. Running for higher office was a difficult decision, Martinez-Rutherford said. “I rethought it 20 different times,” she said. “But, if not now, when? And, if not me, who?” Incidents — like the 2025 killing of a Minnesota state representative —were top of mind, and Martinez-Rutherford said she weighed concerns about her physical safety. “There’s always fear of you know people hating me because I’m trans and threatening (me),” she said. But Martinez-Rutherford said part of her motivation to run came after watching a slew of bills targeting trans people work their way through Wisconsin’s Legislature. That includes legislation that would have banned people assigned male at birth from playing on women’s and girls’ school sports teams, a proposal requiring parental approval before school officials use names or pronouns that differ from a student’s birth certificate and a ban on “gender transition medical intervention,” for minors. Those bills were vetoed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers , but Rutherford-Martinez is well-aware of the fact that she’ll soon be working with many of the Republican lawmakers who sponsored them. “I hope that they see someone in me that maybe changes their hearts,” she said. “Quite honestly, I’m not sure if all of them believe in the rhetoric. It’s just their party that demands it of them.” Rutherford-Martinez will join the Legislature as part of the majority party, after Democrats took control of both the state Assembly and Senate for the first time in 18 years. She’s cited priorities including investing in rapid rehousing to prevent homelessness, expanding the state’s Medicaid program known as BadgerCare, raising Wisconsin’s minimum wage to $20 an hour and overturning Act 10, the 2011 law which curtailed collective bargaining rights for public employees. Across the country, Martinez-Rutherford was among the six candidates who became the first trans or non-binary people elected to their state Legislatures during last week’s midterm elections. After a childhood spent feeling out-of-place, and a young adulthood spent bouncing around the country, Martinez-Rutherford — and her dog Gertrude — have made Madison into a home. “I’m just a normal human who is trying to get through this weird thing we call life,” she said. “I want to be able to live in community and kindness and joy as much as possible, and fight the crap.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board.

Madison has added 2,534 net homes so far in 2026 and is on pace for its strongest year of housing growth since before the pandemic, according to the city. The budget also continues investment in the Triangle Redevelopment Project, part of the city’s broader social housing efforts, and includes funding for violence prevention initiatives and a new body-worn camera program. Other investments include funding for a 10th ambulance company and staffing at the recently opened Imagination Center Library. The budget also provides for fair compensation for city employees, which officials say is important to maintaining city services. Rhodes-Conway said in a press release that the budget avoids new special charges proposed in the city’s five-year operating budget plan, as well as service reductions that could disproportionately affect residents with lower incomes. “There is much to celebrate in next year’s City budget,” Rhodes-Conway says. “In future years, the state-imposed structural deficit will continue to be a major concern for Wisconsin cities.”

Chris Pappas made history this week, becoming the first out gay man to be elected to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, besting Republican candidate Senator John Sununu. Openly transgender Congresswoman Sarah McBride was re-elected by voters in Delaware, besting Republican challenger Joseph Arminio. McBride’s win secures her a second consecutive term representing Delaware in Congress. After first being elected in 2024, making history as the first openly transgender person elected to Congress. Hudgins made history as the state of Georgia’s first out transgender and non-binary state lawmaker, beating out Republican competitor Samantha Boston in House District 90. His win is especially historic as the state hasn’t elected a Democratic candidate in the seat since 1990. Unseating a Republican incumbent in a longstanding red state? Phillip, in this year’s midterms. With her unprecedented win in the state’s House District 25 she became one of three Northern Alabama Democrats to flip seats in the 2026 midterm. Her historic accomplishments include becoming the first openly LGBTQ+ person elected to statewide office in Texas, the first openly LGBTQ+ person elected to the Texas Supreme Court, and, in 2024, the first openly LGBTQ+ woman elected to a Texas appellate court. Mark Pocan will remain in service in Wisconsin, where he ran unopposed for an eighth term as the Democratic U.S. Representative for the state’s 2nd congressional district. Maura Healey was re-elected for a second term, defeating Republican Mike Minogue. title: Jason Ilstrup joins mayoral race, candidates rise to nine - The Daily Cardinal
text: President of nonprofit Downtown Madison Inc. Jason Ilstrup launched his mayoral campaign Nov. 10, bringing the race to nine candidates, many of which are running on the same value done by the  s. Ilstrup is running on a platform of affordable housing, public transportation improvements and public safety. Numerous other candidates noted housing, affordability, police oversight and public trust as priorities in their campaigns. Incumbent Satya Rhodes-Conway cited threats, sexism and harassment as reasons for why she will not be running for reelection. Madison residents disapproved of her handling of the Corey Ruiz shooting, something several candidates highlighted in their campaigns. “We need leadership that listens before it acts, brings people together rather than dividing them and focuses on getting things done,” Syed Abbas wrote on his campaign website. “As mayor, I will work to build a Madison where residents don't have to choose between public safety and social justice — because we deserve both.” Larry “Ace” Williams, who has been mostly silent during the race, made several posts on Instagram showing his support for Ruiz and calling out police brutality. He was the first to file for candidacy Aug. 5 and officially announced his campaign Aug. 13.  Williams was followed by Abbas, Brian Benford, April Kigeya, Kaleem Caire, Marcus Robert Johnson, Natalia Hacerola and Jason Ilstrup, respectively. Ilstrup said he appreciates Rhodes-Conway’s work, having announced his intent to run for mayor one hour after Rhodes-Conway pulled away from the race. “I keep hearing from young families and seniors who can't afford to keep living here,” Ilstrup said at his campaign announcement. “From Black and brown families who still have to work twice as hard for the same opportunities. title: Are trans politics moderating? A new crop of politicians portends a fresh start - UnHerd
text: Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford recently won a seat in Wisconsin's State Assembly. Credit: Vote Dina Nina A few years ago, while shopping in a supermarket in rural Vermont, I observed an interaction between a mother and her teenage son that seemed to encapsulate the nation’s experience with the transgender movement. The son — a large, masculine person — wore pigtails, a schoolgirl miniskirt, and a cropped T-shirt that read “big, fat, trans nightmare” over an exposed, hairy belly. He was flouncing and loud and obviously trying to make a scene, dropping things and telling Mom how much he hated certain foods. The mother, a dowdy small person, endured him with grit-teethed patience — one imagined she’d arranged the outing to help him, or affirm him, the best she knew how. But her task was hopeless: what her son was modeling wasn’t a gender identity or meaningful politics. It was oppositional rage and a victimhood power-grab aimed at ensuring that he be catered to despite any kind of misbehavior. In those “peak-woke” years, gender politics amounted to throwing the same tantrum in our classrooms and before the nation writ large. But a new crop of trans politicians who won elected office this month is flipping the script. They ran as Leftists who happen to be trans, rather than foregrounding a loud and hostile trans identity. It’s difficult to remember, at this point, that being trans wasn’t always an entitlement and a carte blanche to oppress others by making us profess nonsensical things (like the notion that that teenager really was a girl). Feminist and queer theorists like Donna Haraway or Beatriz (now Paul) Preciado have long suggested radical, revolutionary, and political elements to the movement — but in the fine print, those elements were fundamentally incompatible with the power structure. To undermine gender norms was to undermine all hierarchical relations, creating a freer and more equal society, in which no one had too much power, theoretically. That isn’t how things worked out when the movement first went mainstream and gathered power, however. Instead, radical gender politics proved all too genial to the suffocating managerial and HR politics of the 2010s and early 2020s, stoking a backlash in turn. But now, a decisively weaker trans movement may be returning to its utopian and egalitarian roots — and, perhaps, with greater humility than before. By Valerie Stivers And the movement is weaker: the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterms, after all, involved ditching the trans lobby’s more radical demands; and five of seven anti-trans ballot measures, arguably, succeeded. If — a large if , unfortunately — the pediatric gender clinics stay closed and the pronoun police don’t rearm, might trans once again become a meaningful form of egalitarianism or simply a matter of personal choice that isn’t a very big deal in a liberal society? An estimated eight trans people won elections to their state legislatures this cycle, and a few more won hyper-local races. Some attention has been paid to the gender-breakdown — all are biological men. These victories, however, seem to be putting identity politics behind us. The nominees, mostly, didn’t run on trans or LGBT issues, but on working-class economics and street-level social justice. Trust-fund queers posing as people-of-the-people is nothing new, but meaningful action and advocacy for the poor and working class are something different. Democrats won the recent elections on it, and if they can keep their promises, they have a bright future. Some of the trans winners include Bentley Hudgins , who goes by “they,” a union member and human-rights advocate who will represent East Atlanta’s District 90 in Georgia’s House. Hudgins won on an affordability platform. Joanna Whaley , a “she” who won House District 2 outside of Detroit, ran an inclusive campaign that seemed designed to defang the perception that trans people will come for your children and police your speech. Whaley’s campaign material states: “We are a community defined not by the ‘elite,’ but by the people who punch a clock every day to build the products the world relies on.” Whaley wants to repair roads, fix water issues, and address the cost of living. Whaley’s website mentions transgender civil liberties as a top issue, but in the same section vows to protect “free speech, including speech I disagree with.” Coming from a trans politician, this feels like a significant promise. Then there’s Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford , who won more than 90% of the vote in Wisconsin’s State Assembly District 76, which covers Madison. Martinez-Rutherford is “a food-service worker, small-business owner, and a proud transgender woman” who trumpets a work history of being paid $2.33 an hour. The trans candidates have predictable Leftist platforms in many arenas that are of debatable good for working people: some are anti-ICE, which probably means pro-unlimited immigration, and many are anti-school choice, for example. But several also oppose data centers, a working-class issue on both sides of the aisle. Trans identities were once believed to represent this kind of flexibility and category-bridging, creating an inclusive, non-binary politics that was supposed to be inherently anti-capitalist and for the good of the many. Donna Haraway’s “A Cyborg Manifesto,” published in 1985, is often credited with being the foundational work of post-gender social theory. Haraway didn’t speak about trans issues, but she did posit a “cyborg” blend of human and technology that would be the first post-natural creation and thus possess “intimacy with a power that was not generated in the history of sexuality.” Cyborgs’ blurry, uncategorizable “partiality, irony, intimacy, and perversity” would make hierarchies impossible and help mount resistance to “the tradition of racist, male-dominant capitalism.” The cyborg offered the possibility of “converting the laboratories … that spew out the tools of technological apocalypse, and committing to building a political form that actually manages to hold together witches, engineers, elders, perverts, Christians, mothers, and Leninists long enough to disarm the state.” Queer theory picked up these strands, with trans-ness itself becoming the radical cyborg frontier that would precipitate revolution. In 2008’s Testo Junkie , Preciado made the exalted claim that “sex and sexuality [are] the main objects of political and economic activity.” Modern society was transforming gender, sex, and sexuality through “the new dynamics of advanced technocapitalism, global media and biotechnologies,” a regime Preciado called “pharmacopornographic.” Preciado, like Haraway, seemed to believe that leaning into transhumanism would subvert the process. This, despite plentiful evidence that previous forms of body-hacking, like the contraceptive pill, were technologies of control. Preciado wrote that the pill “accentuated the female body as a natural object of intervention.” Pronatalists and Catholic socialists would argue that it funneled women into the workforce at the expense of other human values. Preciado’s personal experiment, recorded in Testo Junkie , was a “voluntary intoxication protocol” in which she added testosterone as “a molecular prostheses” to her “low-tech transgender identity composed of dildos, texts, and moving images.” This personal project, accomplished outside of the medical establishment, would allow the author to “lay claim to the irreducible plurality of my living body … as [a] political site for agency and resistance.” Most of this has turned out to be wishful thinking. Haraway’s claim that “we are all cyborgs now” has come true, in the most literal sense, in the form of the universal human merger with our leash and lover, the smartphone. And Preciado’s pharmacopornographic insight was correct, as well, if we consider the dominion that Big Pharma and Big Porn now maintain over our most intimate selves. But the machines and technologies have served the capitalist, Western-scientific, etc. powers that both wished to resist. “The main trouble with cyborgs,” Haraway wrote, “is that they are the illegitimate offspring of militarism and patriarchal capitalism, not to mention state socialism.” She imagined that they could still be liberatory because “illegitimate offspring are often exceedingly unfaithful to their origins.” Unfortunately, the offspring have proved all too faithful to their corporate and Big Tech origins. By Benjamin Ryan The same can be said of the trans movement, which imagined itself a disruptor but which was embraced by the liberal mainstream with such unseemly haste that its radical vanguard should, at least, have been suspicious. Preciado’s pose in Testo Junkie was to take T illegally, in supposed rebellion against a medical establishment that wished to categorize or diagnose her — a very minor rebellion in 2008, and later simply a pointless one. Moreover, utopians like Preciado and Haraway, who target the oikos , the family, gender, and the body’s reproductive capacities as structures of oppression, are misguided; to the contrary, these human formations are essential structures of resistance. Through its very messy human-ness, the family defies the logics of profit and efficiency. Gender ideology, by contrast, aligns seamlessly with modern neoliberal concerns in terms of destroying these formations. It might also be wishful thinking, then, to see something different in today’s small, local trans winners of seats in their state legislatures. Or it might be a moment in which rapprochement is possible. The hoped-for revolutionary benefits of trans — its valuation of small, human-scale fluidity; its supposed resistance to hierarchical structures; its desire to bridge polarities; its willingness to question — might actually materialize on a more modest scale. The candidates are mostly working class and likable, with a few identitarian exceptions, and many of their causes are good. Many won with huge margins. Preciado stressed the voluntary nature of her intoxication protocol, which seems like an essential feature of the movement that was too quickly lost. In the earliest days of trans, before mothers were terrorized that their children would literally die if not allowed to misbehave in the supermarket — before children’s bodies became a political battleground — there were small communities that agreed to call women men or vice versa, out of love or support or indulgence for the vulnerable and unusual people among us. No one young and vulnerable should be transitioned; trans ideologies should not be forced upon families in schools. But it wasn’t unreasonable to say that trans people have something unique to offer. At the very least, they focus attention on gender, a question that is of the utmost importance and that continues to consume us. They’ve failed as dictators, but as humble leaders, they might offer us an opportunity to practice civility and acceptance, skills the body politic needs more of. Valerie Stivers is a senior editor of UnHerd US.

title: Conservative law firm threatens Madison, Dane County with lawsuit over race- and sex-based ordinances - Channel 3000
text: MADISON, Wis. -- Conservative law firm Wisconsin Institute for Law & Liberty is demanding the City of Madison and Dane County rescind race- and sex-based ordinances or face a lawsuit. In letters sent to Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Dane County Executive Melissa Agard, WILL accused the city and county of enforcing ordinances that the law firm said discriminate against people based on race, ethnicity or sex while giving preferential treatment to others. The letters come after Wisconsin voters passed a new constitutional amendment banning discrimination or preferential treatment by government entities based on race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin. The amendment is expected to go into effect with the Wisconsin Elections Commission certifies the election results. WILL claims that some of the city and county's ordinances violate the new amendment. "It is troubling to many Wisconsinites that several significant ordinances, particularly relating to taxpayer-supported commissions and government contracting, afford Wisconsinites different treatment solely based on their race, ethnicity, or sex," the law firm's managing Vice President Daniel Lennington and deputy counsel Rebecca Furdek said in a letter to Agard. WILL specifically targeted a Madison ordinance that establishes a grant fund for businesses owned by people from historically underrepresented groups and another ordinance that lays out the city's affirmative action policies including the makeup of the Affirmative Action Commission. Under the ordinance, the total number of women, persons with disabilities, and ethnic minority members can never make up less than the majority on the commission. WILL also targeted Dane County ordinances that require the County Executive to ensure that the Equal Opportunity Commission and Commission on Sensitive Crimes have diverse membership as well as other ordinances that lay out the county's Affirmative Action policies. The conservative law firm, which launched a six-figure campaign that in part called for voters to approve the new constitutional amendment, sent letters to 10 other Wisconsin cities and counties as well as the Milwaukee County District Attorney's Office saying they will represent clients in lawsuits filed if certain policies that allegedly violate the new amendment. are not reversed. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. title: Dane County judge, pastor, receives 'graphic' and 'deeply personal' threat - Channel 3000
text: MADISON, Wis. -- Sunday service at Christ the Solid Rock Baptist Church looked different this past weekend. Instead of walking in to see their Senior Pastor, Dane County Circuit Court Judge Everett Mitchell, worshipers arrived to a police presence. "You will see that we do have the Madison Police Department here with us today," Reverend Alfred George told churchgoers before the service began. "They're just here to be with us today, nothing else other than that." Judge Mitchell had made an announcement to the community in the hours ahead of the service on Facebook. Judge Mitchell said he had received "graphic" and "deeply personal" threatening messages the day prior. "The sender said they hoped our church would burn to pieces," Judge Mitchell wrote. Judge Mitchell said the person who sent the threats had come before him in a court case. The pastor and judge said he reported everything to law enforcement, who advised him to stay away from Sunday's service so that his presence didn't draw any danger to worshipers. "I have never faced anything like this in my years on the bench or in the pulpit," Judge Mitchell wrote. "I will not let my work put any of you at risk. I am safe, and I love you." The incident came on the heels of Wisconsin Supreme Court Justice Jill Karofksy's State of the Judiciary , in which she called for more security for judges and courthouses. "Last year I stood here and I told you that the state of our judiciary was troubled. I won't pretend that the threats have gone away. They have not," the chief justice said. Chief Justice Karofsky has said local courthouse security is the top priority in the budget request, which seeks about $3 million over the biennium (2027-29). That money would permanently fund the four statewide officers in the Wisconsin Court Protection Unit, create a Court Security Improvement grant program for counties, and expand the Marshal's Office from one full-time and one part-time position to three full-time positions. Chief Justice Karofsky has asked for security funding for the state's judiciary before. In 2025, Republicans denied the courts that money. That year alone, Wisconsin judges reported 129 threats. That number is reflective of a growing trend of threats against local elected officials nationwide . Last month, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she wouldn't be seeking a third term due to threats and harassment. At the time, the mayor said the price of being in public office had gotten "too high." At the end of his announcement Sunday, Judge Mitchell asked for prayers for his family and the person who sent the threat. title: Threats of political violence require community reckoning - The Badger Herald
text: Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced Oct. 23 she will not be running for reelection this spring. Her announcement, which cited an increase in hostility and threats to herself and local officials in general, is telling of a larger trend of political violence that must be reversed in order to foster a safe environment for political dialogue. Rhodes-Conway’s term as mayor was highlighted by expansions to bus rapid transit, construction of 19,000 homes, growth of the emergency mental health response program and advancements in renewable energy and homeless services, according to The Cap Times. Her leadership also drew criticism around her handling of the police and police oversight. Recently, following the killing of Corey Ruiz by a Madison police officer, under Rhodes-Conway’s direction, the police cleared the encampment that had formed around Ruiz’s memorial and individuals were arrested. However, Rhodes-Conway stated that this did not factor into her decision, according to The Cap Times . Instead, Rhodes-Conway discussed the increased threats and harassment she faced during her term and expressed a desire to focus on her wellbeing. As Madison’s first openly gay mayor and second female mayor, Rhodes-Conway’s election made history, but it also placed her in a position to be harassed with hateful messages. Rhodes-Conway told The Cap Times that she had experienced implicit and explicit sexism in the role and had witnessed the deterioration of civil discourse since she took office in 2019, according to The Cap Times . While Rhodes-Conway noted the increase in right-wing extremism causing hate, she also stated that the political culture more generally has veered toward violence, making life as a public official, especially on a local level, more difficult, according to The Cap Times . Rhodes-Conway is not alone in experiencing the increase in political violence. This hostile political environment impacts elected leaders in many local offices, but the impacts vary among demographics. In the first quarter of 2026, 76% of local officials said they were less likely to engage in key political activities due to fear of threats of violence and harassment. This fear had a disproportionate impact on women, minorities and newly elected officials, according to the Bridging Divides Institute . Local officials should not have to fear their neighbors and community members when doing their jobs. Our local elected officials are dedicated to improving our community, and they should not have to sacrifice their safety for policymaking. This fear is not isolated to local officials. A New York Times investigation found that between 2024 and August 2026, thousands of threats were made to elected officials, forcing them to change their lives in large and small ways. At least 44 governors were targeted and at least half of the members of the House and the Senate faced threats, according to The New York Times . The threats targeted both parties and came in various forms and with varying degrees of specificity, including threats to families and staff members. The investigation found that threats forced officials to change their routines, fortify their homes, remove personal information from the internet and hire personal security. The increased mental and physical cost of running for office in this environment also creates a struggle for party leaders to recruit candidates, especially women, to run for office, according to The New York Times . In 2025, harassment transcended threats and became horrifying acts of violence when Minnesota State House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband were killed in their home by an attacker who possessed a list of dozens of other elected officials to attack, according to ABC News . This target event of political violence had an understandably chilling effect on other elected officials in Minnesota and around the country, causing a moment of reckoning with the state of our political discourse. However, in the year since the shooting, violent threats remain frequent and elected officials are left without an answer to their fears. Some decided to leave office, like Rhodes-Conway and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz who called the shooting of two of his friends and fellow lawmakers an awakening of the price of public office that he is no longer willing to pay. Others remain in the politics space, but with increased security and precautions that make the job more straining and expensive than it was in the past. The irreversible impact of political violence is clear, and we must work as a society to create a system where threats and fear are not in the job description of local elected officials. To do so, we each must evaluate how we speak and think about politics. Politics impact each of our lives in immense ways, but that does not mean we have to approach those we disagree with with vitriol. Instead, we must take an approach that allows for discussion and understanding of our fellow community members, especially when dealing with local politics. Open discussion, empathy and understanding the value of difference are qualities that we should strive for. Before Madison residents consider the candidates’ positions and vote for the next mayor, we must acknowledge the toll of running for office on local candidates. We must cultivate a space where our elected officials not only feel safe when they make policy decisions at City Hall or at the Capitol, but also when they walk their dogs or go to the grocery store. This is a communal effort, and we must all be committed to achieving it.

title: From public servant to storyteller - Isthmus | Madison, Wisconsin
text: Chali Pittman Ald. Sabrina Madison outlined her future plans at a press conference Nov. 1. Would she or wouldn't she? Speculation that Sabrina Madison would run for mayor peaked after Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway reversed course and dropped out of the race for mayor. But Madison has other plans: packing up from a city she’s called home for nearly 20 years, and trying her hand as an independent journalist and storyteller. At a Nov. 1 press conference Madison (the human) described to media and supporters how she had moved to Madison (the city) in 2006, seeking to give her and her son a “fresh start.” At the time, she only knew two people: her manager at Goodwill, where she had been hired as a shift supervisor, and her new landlord on the south side. It was a course on social change at Madison College that introduced her to the ecosystem of local government, organizations and community resources that set the rest of her path. “I had no idea then just how much that experience would shape the rest of my life,” she said. Since then, Madison has created the Black Business Leadership Conference, Black Business Expo, and the Progress Center for Black Women. She’s been named to Essence ’s 100 Woke Black Women and In Business Madison ’s Power 100 , and is a poetry slam winner “with the tattoos to prove it.” Madison was appointed to the city council in 2022 after former Ald. Gary Halverson suddenly resigned , facing backlash to his apparent connection with an extremist group. She told Isthmus at the time she had already been planning a run, disturbed to hear people use “such dehumanizing” language about the permanent men’s homeless shelter (the shelter finally opened in September 2026). “If something bothers me, I don’t like to complain,” she said then. “I act.” She was elected to the seat in 2023 and 2025. That same instinct to act is motivating Madison to launch an independent media outlet focused on local news. The new venture will combine storytelling, photography, writing and video while “humanizing” people whose stories “don’t always get told in an authentic and meaningful way.” It’ll bring Madison (the human) back to Madison (the city) to visit. “I’ll be here,” she says with a laugh in an interview. “I’ll be here more than people are probably going to want me to be here.” She has already enrolled in media, journalism, mass communication and multimedia production classes at Madison College next spring. “I like being in a learning setting,” she says. Those credits will follow her as she completes her degree at the next place she calls home. Her venture will begin with a series called “Sabrina’s Madison,” and Madison says she’s been collecting material for it for years. Her background in local government will also let her home in on investigative projects — as soon as next summer, she’ll be attending local government meetings and decisions as a journalist and storyteller instead of in her capacity as an elected official . Madison says her impetus for the project partly grew out of her interactions with the media as alder, and researching the ethics policies of local newsrooms. Madison says she wants to address what she sees as gaps in the existing local media ecosystem — both in terms of newsroom leadership by Black women and in an understanding of how local government works. Part of her goal is to combat online misinformation, and she’s planning a feature unpacking the basics of local government. She’s playing with calling it “Shit You Should Know.” Madison’s move will take her out of Wisconsin, though she has declined to say where until she’s gone, noting that she’s “learning to save things for myself a little bit more.” But she’s offered one hint: her new home is a place where local culture is focused on baseball. She’s been studying the game. She’s had time. Madison says that she’s been planning her next chapter for more than a year, but the death of a close friend earlier this year, and a need for more flexibility to visit her grandmother, who recently entered memory care, helped convince her to make the jump. “I’ve spent so much of my adult life creating, building, organizing, advocating, showing up, and making things happen for other people,” she said. “I’ve also been thinking about what it would look like to give myself some of that energy and attention.” Madison will also likely dissolve the Progress Center for Black Women. She adds that she’s served plenty of Black women — helping them get press, move into different jobs, get training, and start businesses. “I accomplished my mission,” she adds. “I do not need to continue to ask for money to do the same damn thing.” She adds that Madison’s nonprofit community doesn’t always provide a safety net for people facing financial stress. “The thing I’ve realized…is that Black women need money. That is the primary thing that is driving poor health, poor mental health, stress, evictions,” she says. “All of it is a lack of income.” She says instead of funding nonprofits whose leaders “become wealthy through leading nonprofits,” local governments could do well to assess whether that money could be better spent by directly giving money to those experiencing financial hardship. Madison sought to document her successes in office, along with what she termed “coordinated harassment,” “attempts to bully,” and “outright false narratives,” on posterboard at her Nov. 1 announcement. She gestured to both boards to outline the positives and negatives of being in public service. She included screenshots of social media posts, most critical of her leading role in the October firing of interim independent monitor Aeiramique Glass, on two posterboards, gesturing to them when highlighting the costs of public office: “I have experienced people making assumptions about my intentions, spreading things that aren’t true, and creating narratives about me that have very little to do with the actual work I’ve done,” she said. She also pointed — literally — to her successes. One posterboard was filled with news articles about the Imagination Center, the city library on the northeast side that opened in September . In the audience was Lyle, the constituent who had first pressed Madison to build a new library for her district. He had told her he did not want to wait decades. “I had to make sure that it did not take 50 years,” she said. Ever the self-described “nerd,” there is a theme to Madison’s backup plan if her next venture doesn’t turn out as she hopes. “If it all doesn’t work, I’m gonna go work in the fucking library,” she says. “I’ll be shelving books, and listening to my AirPods.”

title: Corey Ruiz’s family to meet with Dane County DA on Thursday, 4 months after Madison police shooting - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. —  The family of Corey Ruiz will hold a news conference on Thursday following their meeting with the Dane County District Attorney, according to the Ruiz family attorney, Ben Crump.  A news conference with Ruiz’s family and attorneys is expected to follow the meeting to discuss the outcome and next steps in their push for accountability. It comes following a nearly four-month investigation into the incident. The 38-year-old was shot and killed by an police officer on the east side while police were responding to reports of a man checking locked cars. According to Madison police, when officers found Ruiz, he took off on his bicycle and police followed him. Four officers ended up grappling with Ruiz, which is when Madison police allege Ruiz pulled out a knife, slashing an officer. That's when Ruiz was shot, sustaining life-threatening injuries. He was taken to a hospital but later died there. His death sparked protests in Madison and triggered an encampment between Williamson and Baldwin streets, where Ruiz was shot and killed. That encampment was later cleared by police on Aug. 4, which made some protesters upset. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway in a video message defended the decision to clear the encampment, saying there was much to consider, with local businesses and residents caught in the middle. The city did section off a portion of the sidewalk on Baldwin Street for a memorial for Ruiz. Police Chief John Patterson acknowledged the shooting and clearing of the encampment had created a growing rift between the police department and the people of Madison. A funeral for Ruiz was held on Aug. 14, with family members, community supporters and national civil rights leaders renewing calls for justice. The incident also sparked conversations about requiring body-worn cameras for Madison Police Department officers since no body camera footage was captured of the shooting. The fallout from Ruiz's death trickled into leadership positions too. Former Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass was highly involved in the case, launching her own investigation into Ruiz's death. However, Glass was fired in October  following allegations outlined in an August memo from the city attorney’s office that laid out possible violations her office made. Rhodes-Conway announced her decision in October to not seek reelection after receiving threats and being harassed. This story is developing. Check back for updates.
