title: Former Alder Brian Benford formally launches mayoral campaign - Civic Media
text: Former Alder Brian Benford has officially launched his campaign for mayor nearly three months after his initial announcement. Benford originally announced his intent to run for Mayor of Madison near the end of August. While he has been campaigning a bit, he fully launched his campaign Nov. 17 at The Bur Oak, 2262 Winnebago St, and now plans to make larger grassroots efforts in the community. Benford joins a crowded race with nine candidates to date running to replace Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, who will not run for reelection. “When we began this movement, we realized that this isn’t a typical political campaign,” Benford said. “It’s been said before. I’m a 35-year social worker. I’ve served the community for over 35 years, serving children, parents, families, individuals, with the hopes that they could reach their full potential, and in doing so, I would have a chance to reach my full potential.” Benford entered the political realm initially as an alder in 2003 in District 12, re-elected in 2005 and served as District 6’s Alder in 2021. He has served on 19 city committees and led as president of the Equal Opportunities Commission. Benford stepped aside for current Mayor Rhodes-Conway to run for alder in District 12, where she served from 2007 through 2013. He joked, “I would like to think she’s returning the favor,” but doesn’t believe that’s necessarily the case. His campaign’s slogan is “A different kind of campaign. A different kind of leadership.” Benford describes his candidacy as rooted in core values of “truth and reconciliation.” His platform is centered on housing solutions, engaging and centering the community, transportation functionality and equity, honest budget conversations, public health and climate justice. Benford’s bottom line in his campaign is to change the systems in the City that have caused issues in equity. He read off the vision statement from the City of Madison’s website, where he noted that the language is flowery, and it isn’t living up to its message. “In political discourse, we don’t use the word ‘love,’ but we come together in love. That’s what’s sorely missing here in the City of Madison,” Benford said. “What I am going to promise you is I will dedicate every inch of my being to bringing us together, to repairing the damage that’s been done for far too long in the City.” Madison365 asked Benford what’s changed from his initial announcement in August to the official campaign kick-off. Among major events in both Madison and Wisconsin, Mayor Rhodes-Conway announced she would not seek reelection, recent troubles with the Police Civilian Oversight Board, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley elected as governor, a democratic trifecta set to take place next year, and an anticipated announcement from the District Attorney regarding decisions on Corey Ruiz’s death. Ruiz’s death is a motivating factor behind Benford’s choice to run for mayor, but he insists that it is not the sole reason. “I’m not running on Corey’s death. I’m running to prevent other Coreys from being murdered,” Benford said. Benford is running on a push to make large systemic changes, then bow out after a single term. He wants to make it so that community members can be appointed to boards so as to not sway the direction of Madison into the hands of a few elected officials in-grouping with the Mayor. “The way the system is set up, it leads to tampering. Every mayor, not just the current one but every mayor in recent memory, stacks committees with people who align with their policy agendas. I argue that leads to the perpetuation of the status quo. It doesn’t lead to substantial social justice changes,” Benford said. That system also leads to some people who “stay in power way too long,” he continued. “I argue, as a true political leader, it’s important for me once again to find new leaders and give them the tools and skills, rather than hang on to this power,” Benford said. “That’s why right from the beginning I was committed to one term. Most politicians will never say that, and that shows we’re not a politician. We really are sincere about that one term and creating systemic change in the city of Madison.” Benford intends to be the initial catalyst towards the future, not the penultimate change itself. He intends to find new leaders in his tenure, if elected. “We’re gonna identify people that could step into that service, not only the next mayor, but the next Common Council members coming up. I think it’s time for change,” he said. The need for change is clear in who is currently running for mayor, Benford said. The current mayoral race is stacked with around half of its candidates being people of color. “We all know why there’s so many BIPOC people running. That’s a direct reflection on the current state of our city, of our county, of factoring in all the racial disparities that I would argue led to Corey’s murder, of Corey’s life,” Benford said. “It was surrounded and cloaked in the horrendous racial disparities that are in our midst. So we’re done sweeping those things under the rug.” Benford is hopeful that the results of the recent midterms could garner real change, an honest attempt to explore the budget and end the state’s legislative “assault” on Madison. “We have an opportunity to ask the state legislature to stop this assault on the capital city, and we know the history of why that happens because of the Democratic votes that come out of Madison. Now is the time to end this senseless assault on our capital city, where they all work,” he said. Benford plans to hold more rallies, in a primarily grassroots community style, now that his campaign is in full swing. The primary election will be held in February 2027, where the two candidates with the most votes will advance to the April general election. Candidates include Benford, Kaleem Caire, April Kigeya, Syed Abbas, Larry Williams, Johnny Hinds, Marcus Robert Johnson, Natalia Hacerola and Jason Ilstrup. Madison365 is a news outlet covering communities of color in Wisconsin.

title: Madison Braces for Charging Decision in Corey Ruiz Shooting - The Heartland Post
text: Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne is expected to tell Corey Ruiz’s family on Thursday whether he will file criminal charges against Madison police officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, who shot and killed Ruiz on the city’s near east side in July. City officials and police are preparing for protests once the decision is public. Multiple sources told Channel 3000 that Ozanne will meet with the family at 11 a.m. to explain his decision. City officials expect it to be made public shortly after. Ozanne has not publicly confirmed the timing, and WISN said it was still waiting to hear whether the meeting would include charges. MEDIA ALERT: Tomorrow at 1 p.m. CT, @AttorneyCrump will join the family of Corey Ruiz Thursday to meet with the district attorney and medical examiner regarding his fatal police shooting. A news conference will follow to discuss the outcome and next steps in seeking justice. pic.twitter.com/RpbAqJTdSE Family attorney Ben Crump said he will join the family at the meeting with the district attorney and the Dane County medical examiner. The family will then hold a news conference at 1 p.m. at the Center for Black Excellence and Culture, 671 W. Badger Road, to discuss the outcome and next steps in seeking justice and accountability, according to Crump’s office . The decision is Ozanne’s alone. In a July 31 statement , he said the state Division of Criminal Investigation will likely not make a specific recommendation on charging any officer. That decision is left to me. He said he would tell the family first and that any decision cannot be made based on emotion or concern about public reaction. DCI finished its investigation and referred the case to Ozanne by late September, NBC15 reported . In 2015, Ozanne declined to charge Madison officer Matt Kenny in the fatal shooting of Tony Robinson, calling it “a lawful use of deadly police force,” DW reported . In an email to city staff Wednesday, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said officials anticipate protests after the decision. While safety is always our number one priority, individuals wishing to express their feelings and perspectives related to those charging decisions have constitutionally protected rights to protest, vocalize those viewpoints, and gather peacefully, she wrote, according to the Wisconsin State Journal . She said the city would facilitate peaceful protests with as little law enforcement involvement as possible but did not explain what that would mean in practice. Madison officials say they anticipate protests after the Dane County District Attorney’s charging decision in the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. https://t.co/x68MRugiq0 Channel 3000, citing city and law enforcement sources, reported officers will work 12-hour days from Thursday through Thanksgiving. MPD’s Special Events Team, SWAT team, and drone unit will be part of the response. MPD will set up an arrest-processing center, and the Wisconsin State Patrol, UW-Madison Police, the Dane County Sheriff’s Office, and Sun Prairie police are expected to assist. Sources said MPD will not allow major roadways to be blocked for extended periods and will work to prevent barricades and property damage. WISC-TV reports there'll be an arrest-processing center to handle response to Thursday's announcement in the Corey Ruiz death case. Unclear if Dane Co. D.A. Ozanne will charge the MPD officer who shot Ruiz, but protest precautions planned https://t.co/qZ8Gut4pwX ​As of Thursday morning, Heartland Post found no announcement from Gov. Tony Evers or the Wisconsin National Guard placing Guard troops on standby, and no curfew had been announced. Police were called to the Marquette neighborhood on July 22 for a man checking parked vehicles “in an alleged burglary attempt.” He rode off on a bicycle. Four officers caught up with Ruiz, 38, around 1:35 p.m. near South Baldwin and Williamson streets, according to the state Department of Justice account reported by NBC15 . DOJ said Ruiz pulled a knife during a struggle and injured Baitinger-Peterson, two officers tried and failed to use Tasers, and Baitinger-Peterson then fired. Ruiz died at a hospital. Channel 3000 reported he was shot three times, at least once in the head. Bystanders recorded the shooting on cellphones. Madison patrol officers do not wear body cameras, and in September the city moved up its camera rollout to the end of 2027. DOJ named Baitinger-Peterson on Aug. 10. All four officers have been on administrative leave. The Associated Press reported that court records show Ruiz had prior convictions, including felonies for robbery, strangulation and resisting an officer. Protesters built an encampment and barricades at Williamson and Baldwin that police and city crews cleared Aug. 4 . Early estimates put the city’s protest response at about $1 million, Channel 3000 reported. Crump has called the shooting an “execution.” “They not only tackled him, not only tased him, not only kicked him, but you saw they shot him three times in his head and other parts of his body,” he said in July, according to the AP. Police Chief John Patterson said then that “the situation was clearly dangerous.” The Wisconsin Professional Police Association urged the public in July to let the investigation play out, saying “the use of deadly force must be evaluated based on the totality of the circumstances and all available evidence,” Channel 3000 reported . Ozanne also must decide whether to charge former interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass over an Aug. 4 confrontation with officers during the encampment clearing. Channel 3000 reported that the decision is not expected at the same time.

It is disheartening to be reminded that our justice system is imperfect. The narrow focus of whether criminal charges were warranted for this incident doesn't change the fact that Corey Ruiz should be alive and that, in a perfect world, no encounter with the police should end in death. Now that a charging decision has been made, additional investigations can be conducted by the Madison Police Department, the Office of the Independent Monitor, and the Police and Fire Commission. These investigations will focus on whether the officers involved in the death of Corey Ruiz properly followed police protocols and whether discipline, including termination, is appropriate. As your Mayor, I have a responsibility to speak truthfully and frankly. The City of Madison is subject to state and federal law, whether I, the Common Council, or we as a community agree with those laws or not. One of those laws prohibits the Mayor and the Council from suspending, disciplining, or terminating an individual police officer. In my opinion, it's difficult for the Madison Police Department to have the trust of the community while officers involved in shootings remain on the force. But it's not up to me. Only the Madison Police and Fire Commission, a creation of state law, has that authority. I hope they will seriously examine this case and take action. It is essential that our community has confidence in its police department. In an instant, years of building trust through collaborative problem solving and forging genuine connections with residents were erased. To regain trust and bring about real change, we must recognize where the power lies in the criminal justice system and avoid the factionalism that only serves to divide us further. The Madison Police Department must also work with my office, the Common Council, and the public to examine and strengthen policies around de-escalation. I have confidence in Chief John Patterson and believe he is leading his department with sincerity and integrity. To the greatest extent possible, we need to prevent harm by ensuring officers are never placed in a circumstance that requires a split-second decision about use of force. This is essential to protecting our community members, as well as our police officers. I encourage residents to join the multi-faceted effort to strengthen what's already working, adopt additional reforms, and help redefine policing. This is important, not just for Madison, but for our entire country. I'm also deeply concerned that the justified anger and disillusionment caused by this tragedy will result in further harm. Provoking fear and inflicting pain on local businesses and our neighbors solves nothing. It actively diverts resources and time from the bigger, systemic issues we need to be focused on. Please be peaceful if you choose to demonstrate or protest. The power of voicing dissent lies in collective action, not destruction. I implore all of you in Madison to take care of your neighbors, your loved ones, and yourselves during this difficult moment for our city. A different kind of leadership.” Benford describes his candidacy as rooted in core values of “truth and reconciliation.” His platform is centered on housing solutions, engaging and centering the community, transportation functionality and equity, honest budget conversations, public health and climate justice. title: Madison leaders release statements following DA’s decision to not charge officer who shot Corey Ruiz - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Following Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne’s decision not to charge the officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz, local Madison leaders have released statements. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she had strong feelings about the decision and said that Ruiz should be alive and well, mentioning that no encounter with the police should end in death. The mayor said that since the charging decision has been made, additional investigations can be performed by the Madison Police Department, the Office of the Independent Monitor and the Police and Fire Commission. “In my opinion, it’s difficult for the Madison Police Department to have the trust of the community while officers involved in shootings remain on the force,” Rhodes-Conway said. “But it’s not up to me. Only the Madison Police and Fire Commission, a creation of state law, has that authority. I hope they will seriously examine this case and take action.” Rhodes-Conway also highlighted her confidence in Madison Police Chief John Patterson, saying he was leading the department with sincerity and integrity. Rhodes-Conway also told residents to be peaceful and take care of neighbors, their loved ones and themselves during this time. “Provoking fear and inflicting on local businesses and our neighbors solves nothing,” Rhodes-Conway said. “It actively diverts resources and time from the bigger, systemic issues we need to be focused on. Please be peaceful if you choose to demonstrate or protest.” Police Civilian Oversight Board Chair Devon Snyder released a statement, calling Ruiz’s death a tragedy for his family, loved ones and the Madison community. Snyder announced that a loss of life during a police encounter needs transparency, accountability and public confidence. “While the criminal investigation has concluded, many community members continue to have questions about the circumstances surrounding Mr. Ruiz’s death and the processes used to evaluate the incident,” Snyder said. “Criminal investigations serve an important purpose, but they are only one component of accountability. No family should have to question whether an independent review occurred when a loved one dies during a police encounter.” Snyder was concerned that the case reached a conclusion without the benefit of an independent review by an Independent Police Monitor. “Madison’s civilian oversight system was created to provide the community with an additional layer of independent accountability and transparency in exactly these types of cases,” Snyder said. “The absence of an Independent Police Monitor during this critical period represents a significant gap in our oversight framework.” Snyder said the Police Civilian Oversight Board remains committed to advancing transparency, accountability and meaningful civilian oversight. Madison Metropolitan School Board Superintendent Joe Gothard and Board President Savion Castro released a joint statement, explaining that staff is committed to keeping respectful, supportive classroom environments. The district also said they will ensure that all school buildings remain safe, secure and focused on learning. “Our principals and student support teams continue to coordinate and provide any support our school communities need,” MMSD said. “If your student needs support, please encourage them to visit their school’s student services office or contact their school counselor directly. We are deeply grateful to our teachers, principals, and support staff who show up every day to care for our young people and navigate difficult moments alongside them.” The school district said they remain committed to educating and supporting every student in our district. title: No charges for Madison cop who shot Corey Ruiz - Wisconsin Examiner
text: Hundreds of people crowded the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson Streets on Madison’s East Side on July 23 for a vigil in honor of Corey Ruiz, who was killed by a Madison Police officer July 22. On Thursday Dane County DA Ismael Ozanne announced he will not charge the officer involved. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner) No charges will be filed against Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, the Madison police officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets on July 22, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne announced Thursday. Officers responded to the area after receiving reports that someone had been looking into parked cars. When four officers tried to arrest Ruiz in the intersection, a struggle ensued and officers reported that he had pulled a knife. Ruiz was tased before being shot at close range. Ruiz’s killing sparked weeks of protest in Madison this summer, including the occupation of the busy intersection by activists. In the months since Ruiz was killed, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would not be running for re-election, citing threats she’d received following the shooting. City officials have also been in an ongoing fight with Madison’s independent police monitor since Ruiz’s death. That fight has included disputes over the role and authority of the position to investigate the shooting and the firing of the interim monitor by the city’s common council. On Thursday, Ruiz’s family met with Ozanne and the county medical examiner and were informed of the decision not to file charges. In a statement, the family’s attorney Ben Crump argued the available video of the incident shows an excessive use of force. “There is nothing in the videos the district attorney showed us that justifies this officer stepping back, pulling his gun, and firing three shots at point-blank range at Corey Ruiz after he had been tased and was on the ground, hitting him once in the chest and with the kill shot to his head,” Crump said. “The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived. It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.” In a news release, Ozanne said that the shooting was justified because Ruiz had pulled a knife and therefore Baitinger-Peterson had a genuine fear that Ruiz presented a deadly threat. “A knife can be used as a dangerous weapon and may pose a grave danger of bodily harm and/or death to an individual. A person fleeing from police who, when contacted, physically resists and produces a knife from their person does pose a threat of great bodily harm and/or death to the officers,” Ozanne said. “Responding to that threat with deadly force is permitted under the law. A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand. The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.” At a press conference Thursday afternoon at Madison’s Center for Black Excellence and Culture, Ruiz’s family, including his siblings, mother and daughter, expressed disappointment and frustration that the officer won’t be held accountable for what they see as a miscarriage of justice. Crump said he and the family would explore “every possible legal remedy” available to them, adding that “when you look at that video, this video cries out for a civil rights lawsuit.” Some local elected officials also criticized Ozanne’s decision. I am committed to public safety and real justice for all – and to reforming our broken criminal justice system that is not serving Wisconsinites well or fairly. A miscarriage of justice against one of us is an injustice to us all.” This story has been updated. title: District attorney won’t charge Madison police officer in shooting of Corey Ruiz - WPR
text: The Dane County district attorney won’t bring charges against any of the officers involved after a Madison police officer fatally shot Corey Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man , on July 22. The county’s top prosecutor, Ismael Ozanne, made the announcement on Thursday afternoon. “I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody,” Ozanne said in a news release. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Members of the Ruiz family met earlier in the day with Ozanne and the county’s medical examiner. During a news conference Thursday, Corey’s mother, Elsa Ruiz, spoke through sobs. “I have to live with every day (of) him not being here,” she said. “It hurts so bad not to have him here … He was loved. He was cared for.” Ben Crump, an attorney for the Ruiz family, said the district attorney should have filed charges. “We don’t believe any of the shots were justified,” Crump told reporters. “Not the first shot, not the second shot and definitely not the third shot. The kill shot to his head was not justified. It was the textbook definition of excessive use of force.” The Division of Criminal Investigation within Wisconsin’s Department of Justice investigated the incident and handed its results over to Ozanne’s office. A 2014 state law mandates that an outside agency investigates an “officer-involved death.” After the shooting, the city placed a total of four officers involved with Ruiz’s attempted arrest on paid administrative leave. Those officers will remain on leave while internal and external investigations into their conduct are ongoing, Madison Police Chief John Patterson said. “I trust our officers to make the best possible decisions in the worst possible moments,” Patterson said Thursday at a separate news conference. “So many times, officers’ decisions are limited by the circumstances they face, circumstances out of their control. I think these reviews will help ensure MPD’s policies and procedures are aligned with community expectations and best practices.” In late October, Patterson announced that the police department has brought on two professors with the University of South Carolina to review its use of force recommendations. That work will begin in January 2027, and will result in a report with recommendations for improvement, according to MPD. In the months since the shooting, protestors have been calling for the arrest of Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, the officer who fired the fatal shots . The shooting took place in the early afternoon at the intersection of South Baldwin and Williamson streets, known to Madison residents as Willy Street. According to the DCI and Madison police, Ruiz pulled out a knife during a struggle with police, which led to Baitinger-Peterson being injured. Ozanne’s news release did not give details about Baitinger-Peterson’s injuries. Patterson said Thursday he saw photos showing cuts on the outside of Baitinger-Peterson’s hands. Ozanne wrote in his press release that toxicology reports found Ruiz had methamphetamine in his system at the time of the shooting, as well as chemicals associated with cocaine and cannabis. The interaction began when Ruiz fled on a bike after police responded to reports about a man who was checking car doors and to a report of an alleged attempted burglary , the DCI said. Multiple bystanders took cellphone video of the end of that police encounter, and those videos immediately began circulating online, provoking outrage within the city. The bystander video shows Ruiz approaching the intersection on a bike before falling off the bike onto the pavement, as multiple officers try to detain him. While Ruiz is down on the pavement, the video shows an officer — later identified as Baitinger-Peterson — firing a total of three shots. Ruiz was “hit with two of the three shots; once in the torso and once in the head,” Ozanne’s news release said. During the incident, two other officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz, but that Taser didn’t work properly, according to the DCI and Madison’s police chief . “One set of Taser prongs made contact with Mr. Ruiz’s left hand,” Ozanne wrote in his news release. “The other set of Taser prongs were on Mr. Ruiz’s left side. Mr. Ruiz fell or was taken to the ground just before three shots were fired by an officer.” Patterson told reporters he still has questions about what transpired with those stun weapons. “I still don’t know exactly what happened with the Taser,” the police chief said. Attorneys for the Ruiz family questioned why shots were necessary while Ruiz was already on the ground. And they indicated that further legal action is coming. “When you look at that video, this video cries out for a civil rights lawsuit,” Crump said. After the shooting, Madison saw a wave of protests at locations including the state Capitol . Mourners set up a makeshift memorial in the intersection where he was shot. That memorial morphed into multi-block encampment, with tents, mattresses and grills. The encampment blocked traffic in the area for nearly two weeks, before Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway made the decision to have it forcibly cleared on Aug. 4 . The mayor cited harm to nearby residents and businesses. Before officials cleared the intersection, people who were homeless and living at the encampment were given vouchers to stay temporarily at nearby hotels, the mayor said. Madison’s former interim Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass pledged to complete her own investigation into the shooting. The police monitor’s office demanded records related to the incident , including dashboard camera footage. However, the city attorney’s office said that, because of state law, Madison could not legally release those records without the approval of DCI and the Dane County District Attorney . In October, Madison’s Common Council voted 14-6 to fire Glass, citing problems with her job performance . As part of that vote, alders directed the Council’s chief to take over Glass’ duties on an interim basis. Madison’s Police Civilian Oversight board has since tapped former City Alder Rebecca Kemble to serve as interim monitor, teeing up a legal dispute with the city attorney’s office. Earlier this year, Green Bay Police recommended that Glass be charged with obstructing and resisting an officer, as well as battery to an officer, following a physical altercation with Madison police at the site of a protest near where Ruiz was shot. An external police agency investigated because of Madison officers’ involvement in the incident. Glass has denied wrongdoing in that incident. So far, Ozanne has not announced whether or not his office will file charges against Glass. Glass spoke during the news conference called by the Ruiz family on Thursday. Meanwhile, a local political action committee is asking Madison’s Police and Fire Commission to fire Baitinger-Peterson. The complaint filed by Blacks for Political and Social Action of Dane County accuses Baitinger-Peterson of violating city policies, ordinances and Wisconsin laws related to use of force, deescalation and professional conduct. It also calls for the other officers involved in the arrest to be fired or suspended. Baitinger-Peterson has just over a decade of law enforcement experience, and was first hired by the Madison Police Department in 2015. Prior to the shooting of Ruiz, Baitinger-Peterson had never used deadly force, according to Madison’s police chief . The chief also said in August that there have been no sustained use of force allegations against Baitinger-Peterson during Baitinger-Peterson’s time with the department. In a statement Thursday evening, Governor-elect David Crowley said he “recognize(s) the pain and frustration many people are feeling … especially in communities of color that have watched similar tragedies unfold for generations.” “People have every right to be upset and to make their voices heard,” said Crowley, who noted in the statement that he will be Wisconsin’s first Black governor. “I encourage the community to continue speaking out and demanding answers, but to do so peacefully. More violence will not bring Corey back or change the District Attorney’s decision. It will only add to the pain of a community already carrying so much.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board.

Madison is Wisconsin's second-largest police department, according to federal data. It is the only police department among the state's 15 largest without bodycams. The fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz reignited the debate over why the Madison Police Department did not have bodycams. Last week, the Madison Common Council approved a 2027 budget that invests in a new bodycam program . Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway requested nearly $415,000 , spread across the next three years, for police bodycams in her budget proposal. The backstory: Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers responded to calls about a man stealing bicycles and checking car doors and confronted him on July 22, but he rode away on a bicycle. Police later encountered the man again, at Baldwin and Williamson, and the man "fell or was pulled off the bicycle." There was a struggle in the middle of the intersection, and police said the man pulled out a knife and injured an officer. Officers used a taser to try to take the man into custody before the injured officer shot the man, since identified as Corey Ruiz. Ruiz was pronounced dead at a hospital. The Wisconsin Department of Justice identified the officer who shot and killed Ruiz as Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, who has more than 10 years of law enforcement service. Baitinger-Peterson is among four officers involved who were placed on administrative leave as the DOJ's Division of Criminal Investigation investigates the shooting as a homicide . Protests in the streets of Madison, including an encampment at the intersection where Ruiz was shot, continued for weeks after Ruiz's death. title: Madison officer won’t face charges in Ruiz shooting - Wisconsin Law Journal
text: Women in the Law USA Today Network // November 20, 2026 // Madison officer won’t face charges in Ruiz shooting Prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump during a news conference conference after the Dane County District Attorney decided not to charge a police officer is the shooting death of Corey Ruiz Thursday in Madison. (USA Today Network) USA Today Network // November 20, 2026 // Listen to this article IN BRIEF Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne announced Nov. 19 that Madison police officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson will not face criminal charges in the July 22 fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz, 38, citing the officer’s fear of deadly force. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump , representing Ruiz’s family, criticized the decision and said the family is exploring other legal options, including a potential civil rights lawsuit alleging excessive force. Madison police will conduct an internal use-of-force review and an outside sentinel review of the shooting. Dane County’s top prosecutor on Thursday declined to charge a Madison police officer for a July shooting of a 38-year-old man that had shocked and angered many in Wisconsin’s capital. Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne cited Corey Ruiz being armed with a knife, resisting arrest and the fact that he was not stopped by officers’ attempts to use a stun gun on him as his reasons for declining to file charges against officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, he said in a statement announcing his decision. “A person does not have to like and [or] agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” Ozanne’s statement said. Ruiz’s family is represented by prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who said he was exploring other legal avenues, including a civil rights lawsuit. In a statement he said the officer shooting Ruiz was “clearly an excessive use of force.” “We believe the district attorney should’ve charged this officer for killing Corey Ruiz,” Crump said at a Nov. 19 press conference. Ozanne’s decision was met with backlash from Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, who called it “disheartening.” She said the four officers involved in the shooting remaining employed by the department made it difficult for the community to trust the city’s police. Only the city’s Police and Fire Commission has authority to fire a police officer. “The narrow focus of whether criminal charges were warranted for this incident doesn’t change the fact that Corey Ruiz should be alive and that, in a perfect world, no encounter with the police should end in death,” she said. Ruiz’s shooting will now undergo an internal use-of-force review done by an outside expert and a sentinel review by an outside organization on the department’s handling of the shooting, Madison Police Chief John Patterson said. Those will likely not be released until next year and the officers involved will remain on administrative leave during the internal review, Patterson said, while declining to offer his opinion on the shooting. Patterson said Ruiz’s family deserves compassion and empathy. He also defended the department’s officers. “I trust our officers to make the best possible decisions in the worst possible moments,” Patterson said. Family members remembered Ruiz at a funeral as a lover of music and beloved family member. He struggled with mental health issues and drug use at points in life. His family has been harshly critical of the shooting. Gov. Tony Evers said he was thinking of Ruiz, his family and those who knew him. “I know there are many Wisconsinites who are angry and frustrated to learn that the district attorney will not be seeking criminal charges,” Evers said on social media. “I join Corey’s family in strongly encouraging engagement to remain peaceful as work continues for change within our criminal justice system.” In his four-page statement, Ozanne, who described the shooting as a tragedy, included a description of the events that preceded Ruiz’s shooting and how he came to his decision. Baitinger-Peterson shot Ruiz during a July 22 encounter where four officers attempted to arrest the man after Ruiz fled officers. Police sought him after a report he had attempted to open vehicle doors and an attempted burglary. An initial responding officer was familiar with Ruiz and called for backup before attempting to make contact with him, Ozanne’s statement said. Baitinger-Peterson shot at him three times, and struck him twice, as the other officers attempted to restrain him. The shooting came as officials said two other officers previously used a stun gun on Ruiz, but it was ineffective. “Any person may use deadly force to respond to a genuine fear of deadly force to that person or any other person,” Ozanne said in his statement. The state Department of Justice’s Department of Criminal Investigation released its nearly 1,800-page investigative file following Ozanne’s announcement. Included in that were details from a July 31 interview with Baitinger-Peterson, who told state investigators he feared Ruiz would stab him and other officers. “PO Baitinger-Peterson was not sure what would happen because he knew the subject had a deadly weapon,” the file reads. “PO Baitinger-Peterson transitioned to his handgun as [he] believed deadly force was his only option. PO Baitinger-Peterson feared for his life and the lives of the other officers because they were so close to the subject with the knife.” Results from a toxicology report included in Ozanne’s statement showed Ruiz had methamphetamine and substances that indicate cocaine use in his system. Ozanne’s statement made no reference to Baitinger-Peterson being injured by a knife Ruiz wielded during the struggle. That is in contrast to the public’s previous understanding of the shooting, where Madison officials previously said the officer was injured by the knife during the struggle. Patterson said at a press conference Nov. 19 that he saw wounds to both of one officer’s hands, but did not identify which officer. The DOJ’s investigative files indicate Baitinger-Peterson was injured, but the specifics of those injuries are redacted. No charges will be filed against the other three officers involved as well, Ozanne said. Crump was scathing in his criticism of Ozanne’s decision at a Nov. 19 press conference, held at Madison’s Center For Black Excellence and Culture. Family, numerous community members, media and others packed the room. Rep. Shelia Stubbs, D-Madison, attended, as did former interim police monitor Aeiramique Glass. Crump said county medical staff told them that Ruiz would have survived if the second striking gunshot, which struck Ruiz in the head, had not been fired. He disputed there was any relevance to the events that occurred before Ruiz was shot and argued the stun guns did work. Ozanne showed him and the family various videos and commentary to explain his decision. “In the video you see that they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him,” Crump said. “The video is the unbiased objective witness.” Ruiz’s family criticized the decision as well. Many people during the press conference chanted “we love you” to members of the family as they spoke. “This is so wrong. They have no idea what I have to live with every day, him not being here,” Ruiz’s mother, Elsa, said. “It hurts so bad.” Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley said Ruiz’s shooting raises “serious questions” about officers’ use of force. He said he would work to improve police use-of-force and how police shootings are investigated. “We cannot change what happened to Corey, but we can take responsibility for making sure his death leads to a serious conversation about how we move forward so that every Wisconsinite can have confidence that they will be treated with dignity and fairness, regardless of their race or ZIP code,” Crowley said in a statement. Ozanne’s decision was also criticized by state Sen. Kelda Roys, D-Madison, who described it in a statement as a “miscarriage of justice.” State Sen. Dora Drake, D-Milwaukee, also criticized the decision. “The Dane County District Attorney’s decision not to prosecute the officer who killed Corey Ruiz is deeply disappointing, and yet another example of a justice system that fails to hold the powerful to account,” Roys said. Former Democratic candidate for Wisconsin governor Francesca Hong said Ozanne’s decision was “disturbing.” “He and his family deserve equal rights under the law. Denying victims of police violence equal treatment under the law is wrong,” she posted on social media. Graphic and startling footage of the shooting spread rapidly on social media and protests roiled Madison after it occurred. The day after the shooting, Madison’s mayor, Rhodes-Conway, and other officials said Ruiz’s death necessitated a review of department policies. Police Chief Patterson acknowledged the shooting damaged trust between police and the community. “I want to be clear. It does not matter who you are or what your past is. You should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement,” Rhodes-Conway said during a July 23 press conference. An encampment was erected near the site of the shooting, on the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets following the shooting. That encampment remained for about two weeks, before city workers and police cleared the area in early August. Public officials like Rhodes-Conway and Patterson called on people to remain peaceful following Ozanne’s decision. Many who protested the shooting pointed to it as an example of the disproportionate force by police used against Black people in Madison and elsewhere. That was repeated at the Ruiz family press conference Thursday. “Racism is still out there,” said Ruiz’s 13-year-old daughter, Kah’liyah Aliomar. The shooting of Ruiz prompted a renewed and successful push for Madison police officers to be outfitted with body cameras, a relatively standard practice across large police departments in the country. Madison’s council members passed its 2027 budget with funding to implement that program. The shooting was investigated by the Wisconsin Department of Justice ‘s Division of Criminal Investigation. Investigators from that agency forwarded its findings to Ozanne’s office. A DOJ spokesperson told the Journal Sentinel he had no immediate comment on the decision. title: Madison police shooting : No charges for officers , officials react
text: MADISON, Wis. - The Dane County District Attorney's Office announced no criminal charges will be filed against the Madison police officers involved in the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz. The decision prompted reaction from lawmakers and leaders. Big picture view: Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozane determined Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson's use of deadly force was "reasonable," and none of the officers involved would be criminally charged .  FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android Ozane concluded "it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody." Related article Madison police shooting: No charges for officer in Corey Ruiz's death The Madison police officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz this summer will not be criminally charged, the Dane County District Attorney's Office determined. What they're saying: FOX6 News has received statements from elected officials and organizations on the district attorney's decision. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway: "Like many in our community, I have strong feelings about the Dane County District Attorney's charging decision. It is disheartening to be reminded that our justice system is imperfect. The narrow focus of whether criminal charges were warranted for this incident doesn't change the fact that Corey Ruiz should be alive and that, in a perfect world, no encounter with the police should end in death. "Now that a charging decision has been made, additional investigations can be conducted by the Madison Police Department, the Office of the Independent Monitor, and the Police and Fire Commission. These investigations will focus on whether the officers involved in the death of Corey Ruiz properly followed police protocols and whether discipline, including termination, is appropriate. "As your Mayor, I have a responsibility to speak truthfully and frankly. The City of Madison is subject to state and federal law, whether I, the Common Council, or we as a community agree with those laws or not. One of those laws prohibits the Mayor and the Council from suspending, disciplining, or terminating an individual police officer. In my opinion, it's difficult for the Madison Police Department to have the trust of the community while officers involved in shootings remain on the force. But it's not up to me. Only the Madison Police and Fire Commission, a creation of state law, has that authority. I hope they will seriously examine this case and take action. "It is essential that our community has confidence in its police department. In an instant, years of building trust through collaborative problem solving and forging genuine connections with residents were erased. To regain trust and bring about real change, we must recognize where the power lies in the criminal justice system and avoid the factionalism that only serves to divide us further. "The Madison Police Department must also work with my office, the Common Council, and the public to examine and strengthen policies around de-escalation. I have confidence in Chief John Patterson and believe he is leading his department with sincerity and integrity. To the greatest extent possible, we need to prevent harm by ensuring officers are never placed in a circumstance that requires a split-second decision about use of force. This is essential to protecting our community members, as well as our police officers. I encourage residents to join the multi-faceted effort to strengthen what's already working, adopt additional reforms, and help redefine policing. This is important, not just for Madison, but for our entire country. "I'm also deeply concerned that the justified anger and disillusionment caused by this tragedy will result in further harm. Provoking fear and inflicting pain on local businesses and our neighbors solves nothing. It actively diverts resources and time from the bigger, systemic issues we need to be focused on. Please be peaceful if you choose to demonstrate or protest. The power of voicing dissent lies in collective action, not destruction. "I implore all of you in Madison to take care of your neighbors, your loved ones, and yourselves during this difficult moment for our city." Madison Police Chief John Patterson: Full press conference from the Madison Police Department following the decision to not press charges against the officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz State Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Madison) "The Dane County District Attorney's decision not to prosecute the officer who killed Corey Ruiz is deeply disappointing, and yet another example of a justice system that fails to hold the powerful to account. This is not an isolated failure by prosecutors to uphold the rights of every citizen. Rather, it reflects a broader pattern of policing and prosecutorial decisions that deny those harmed by police violence equal treatment under the law and accountability when their most fundamental rights are violated. "I am committed to public safety and real justice for all – and to reforming our broken criminal justice system that is not serving Wisconsinites well or fairly. A miscarriage of justice against one of us is an injustice to us all." State Rep. Shelia Stubbs (D-Madison): "Today, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne announced that Madison Police Department Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson will not be criminally charged for fatally shooting Corey Ruiz on July 22, 2026. "Following the decision, I joined Civil Rights Attorney Ben Crump, Corey Ruiz’s loved ones, and community advocates for a press conference at the Center for Black Excellence and Culture in my district in order to show my support to the Ruiz family. "My heart, my thoughts, and my prayers remain with Ms. Elsa Ruiz and the rest of Corey Ruiz’s family, friends, loved ones, and community as they begin to process this devastating news. "I am shocked to have learned that there will be no criminal charges for the officer who took the life of a son, brother, father, and member of this community. "This is not the decision this community was expecting, and it is one that will have lasting detrimental impacts on our city and the trust between residents of color and law enforcement. Once again, the people of Madison are put into a position of trying to make sense of a senseless act. "We must be persistent in our calls for transparency, accountability, and full justice for Corey Ruiz and his family. I will continue to stand with the family and support them as they navigate this very emotional time following the District Attorney’s decision." Madison Police Civilian Oversight Board Chair Devon Snyder: "Today, the District Attorney announced that no criminal charges will be filed against the officer involved in the death of Corey Ruiz. Regardless of one's view of this decision, the death of Corey Ruiz remains a profound tragedy for his family, loved ones, and the Madison community. The loss of life during a police encounter demands transparency, accountability, and public confidence in the systems responsible for reviewing police conduct. "While the criminal investigation has concluded, many community members continue to have questions about the circumstances surrounding Mr. Ruiz's death and the processes used to evaluate the incident. Criminal investigations serve an important purpose, but they are only one component of accountability. No family should have to question whether an independent review occurred when a loved one dies during a police encounter. "As Chair of the Police Civilian Oversight Board, I am deeply concerned that this case reached its conclusion without the benefit of an independent review by an Independent Police Monitor. Madison's civilian oversight system was created to provide the community with an additional layer of independent accountability and transparency in exactly these types of cases. The absence of an Independent Police Monitor during this critical period represents a significant gap in our oversight framework. "The Police Civilian Oversight Board remains committed to advancing transparency, accountability, and meaningful civilian oversight. The community deserves more than the conclusion of a criminal investigation. The community deserves a civilian oversight system that is fully operational, independent, and capable of carrying out the responsibilities entrusted to it. "Our thoughts remain with the Ruiz family and all those affected by this tragedy. Accountability is not defined by a single decision. It is demonstrated through a continued commitment to transparency, independent oversight, and meaningful reform." Gov. Tony Evers: Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers released a statement reacting to the Dane County District Attorney's Office decision to not bring charges against the police officer who shot Corey Ruiz. He asked for action tonight to remain peaceful. Governor-elect David Crowley: "My heart is with Corey Ruiz's family and everyone in the Madison community who continues to grieve his loss.   "The video of Corey's killing is deeply troubling and raises serious questions about the force used against him. I recognize the pain and frustration many people are feeling following the District Attorney's decision, especially in communities of color that have watched similar tragedies unfold for generations.  "People have every right to be upset and to make their voices heard. I encourage the community to continue speaking out and demanding answers, but to do so peacefully. More violence will not bring Corey back or change the District Attorney's decision. It will only add to the pain of a community already carrying so much.  "As Wisconsin's first Black governor-elect, I understand that these incidents are part of a much longer history that has left generations of Americans questioning whether our justice system values their lives equally and whether law enforcement officers are held to the same standards as everyone else.  "When Corey was killed, I spoke about the deep wounds these incidents reopen and the work ahead to restore trust in our institutions. I stand by those words today. We must respect the independence of the criminal justice system, but the decision not to file charges does not end the conversation or resolve the questions this tragedy has raised. "As governor, I will use this office to look beyond this one case and examine what we can do differently to prevent tragedies like this from happening again. That means reviewing how officer-involved deaths are investigated and how information is shared with families and the public. It also means taking a hard look at use-of-force policies and training, while listening to the communities most affected by these encounters.   "I will work with lawmakers, law enforcement and community leaders to identify meaningful changes that can make our justice system more transparent and help rebuild public trust. We cannot change what happened to Corey, but we can take responsibility for making sure his death leads to a serious conversation about how we move forward so that every Wisconsinite can have confidence that they will be treated with dignity and fairness, regardless of their race or ZIP code. That is the standard our state must work toward, and I am committed to it." State Sen. Julian Bradley (R-New Berlin): "Police officers have one of the toughest jobs there is, and they have every right to defend themselves. Today’s decision shows why we SHOULD let investigations play out instead of rushing to judgement on social media." State Sen. Dora Drake (D-Milwaukee) "The people calling for justice for Corey Ruiz know the truth: that he should still be alive today. Since this summer, there were millions of views online of people watching multiple Madison Police Officers hold Mr. Ruiz down before one officer chose to shoot him from point-blank range. The Dane County District Attorney’s decision today is not only disturbing but continues to amplify the mistrust in our legal institutions. Continuing to deny victims of violence equal treatment under the law, regardless of who you are, will never allow our state to fully heal. Corey’s family was denied their day in court. Now, as elected leaders, it is our duty to reform this flawed system to ensure that the law is equally applied to everyone."  Milwaukee County Board Supervisors Shawn Rolland, Juan Miguel Martinez, Caroline Gómez-Tom, Leevan D. Roundtree Jr., Anne O’Connor, Willie Johnson Jr., First Vice-Chair Steven Shea and Second Vice-Chair Priscilla E. Coggs-Jones: "If it takes five months to determine if charges are warranted, most people would think there’s enough evidence to let a jury decide. This is what juries are for. Let a jury do its job. We’ve all seen the video. This is not a decision most Wisconsinites want to see made behind closed doors. That evidence deserves its day in court." ACLU of Wisconsin Executive Director Melinda Brennan: "Today in Madison, we witnessed history tragically repeat itself. Police violence has been claiming the lives of Black and Brown people for as long as this country has existed. It is a generations-long legacy that persists to this day, over and over again, often with impunity.  Corey Ruiz’s life mattered, and he deserved help with the hardships he faced. Instead, he was shot to death in the middle of the street.  Too often, our unhoused neighbors or those struggling with mental health difficulties are met with a response from police rather than what they actually need – more resources, community-based support, and options for care and treatment opportunities. People navigating these issues are more likely to be subject to dangerous and deadly police encounters, especially if they are people of color. If we’re serious about building communities where everyone can thrive, we must invest in the solutions that meaningfully address peoples’ needs and not simply rely on policing as the answer to everything. Corey Ruiz should still be alive, and we can honor his life by continuing to do the work necessary to make sure this never happens again. Our hearts go out to Corey’s loved ones – along with everyone in the community grieving with a pain that feels all too familiar – and we stand in solidarity with those demanding systemic change." Wisconsin Professional Police Association Executive Director Jim Palmer: "We believe the district attorney's determination that Officer Baitinger-Peterson's use of deadly force was legally justified is supported by the evidence and consistent with the legal standards governing the use of force by law enforcement officers. "As the independent investigation has established, officers were responding to multiple reports of criminal activity when they encountered Mr. Ruiz. As an officer attempted to detain him, Mr. Ruiz produced a large, kitchen-style knife from his clothing. Despite the efforts of additional officers to gain control of the situation, including the use of less-lethal measures, Mr. Ruiz continued to resist while armed with the knife. These circumstances are central to understanding the immediate danger confronting the officers and the rapidly evolving decisions they were required to make. "Today's announcement also underscores the importance of allowing independent investigations to proceed without prejudging their conclusions. Wisconsin has long recognized that incidents involving the use of deadly force by law enforcement demand a thorough and impartial examination of the facts. That process exists to ensure that decisions are grounded in evidence and the law, rather than speculation, public pressure, or preconceived conclusions. "Unfortunately, much of the public discussion surrounding this incident occurred before the investigation was completed and before all of the relevant facts were known. While public scrutiny of law enforcement is both appropriate and necessary, accountability must be grounded in a fair and objective assessment of the evidence. Officers, like the members of the communities they serve, deserve nothing less. "While the facts and circumstances of this incident necessarily guide today's determination, we recognize the profound loss that Mr. Ruiz's death represents to his family and loved ones, as well as the significant impact this incident has had on the broader Madison community. We appreciate that a finding that an officer's actions were legally justified does not diminish that loss or the grief experienced by those affected. "We also recognize the extraordinary toll this incident has taken on the officers involved and their families. These officers cooperated with the independent investigation while enduring intense public scrutiny, threats, and personal harassment. Regardless of one's views about this incident, threats against officers or their families are unacceptable and have no place in a community committed to public safety and the rule of law. "As Madison moves forward, we hope today's announcement provides an opportunity to replace division and speculation with a more constructive dialogue about public safety, accountability, and the difficult realities confronting law enforcement officers. The WPPA remains committed to supporting its members and strengthening the relationship between law enforcement and the communities they serve. "We will carefully review the district attorney's findings and will be prepared to address additional questions as appropriate." title: Madison proposing full ban on hyperscale data center construction - WTMJ
text: MADISON, Wis. — With its one-year moratorium on data center construction set to expire early in 2027, the City of Madison is now preparing to go a step further and fully ban the construction of hyperscale campuses within city limits. The city’s one-year data center moratorium, described when approved in 2025 as a first-of-its-kind move in Wisconsin, is set to expire on January 24, 2027. Rather than extend the moratorium, the City is moving for a much wider-reaching plan that in addition to the hyperscale ban would impose severe restrictions on all other forms of data center building plans. “Madison residents are rightly concerned that a powerful industry will foist a data center on our community without accountability or regard for the potential negative impacts. This strong proposal will prevent that from happening,” said Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway in a release November 20. “It also accounts for responsible and legitimate uses of computing power, which already occur in Madison without causing problems. With this proposal, the City is effectively exercising its authority, and I strongly urge State lawmakers to enact sensible data center regulation so local communities have additional tools to protect residents.” The moratorium cannot legally be extended indefinitely to prevent data center development, said Rhodes-Conway. As proposed, the ordinance places several layers of restrictions and regulations on the development of any new data centers in Madison: The proposal’s legislative process will begin with its first review before the City Plan Commission November 30. It would also need to go before the Business and Economic Resources Committee December 16 and the Sustainable Madison Committee December 21, with each taking public comment. It is scheduled to be before the Common Council January 12, 2027.

title: Madison Common Council set to propose new ordinance further restricting data center development - WKOW
text: MADISON (WKOW) -- The Madison City Council is preparing to introduce an ordinance that would further limit data center development within the city. An announcement from the city on Friday said that the City's one-year moratorium is set to expire on January 24, 2027. The proposed ordinance would place several restrictions and regulations on new data center development. The current moratorium cannot legally be extended indefinitely. "Madison residents are rightly concerned that a powerful industry will foist a data center on our community without accountability or regard for the potential negative impacts. This strong proposal will prevent that from happening," Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said. "It also accounts for responsible and legitimate uses of computing power, which already occur in Madison without causing problems." Restrictions listed in the proposal include; a total ban on hyperscale data centers, a total ban on data centers in residential zones, a hard cap on maximum size of data centers, a requirement for center developers to comply with noise ordinances, and requirement of external mechanical equipment or backup generators. The introduction of the proposal will take place during the next Common Council meeting on Nov. 24. Following the introduction, the ordinance has several steps before becoming law, but is expected to have a final vote on January 12, 2027, according to the announcement on Friday. There are no active proposals for a data center in Madison and no applications have been submitted.
