title: Step by Step: Why the Madison Officer Who Shot Corey Ruiz Was COMPLETELY JUSTIFIED - Wisconsin Right Now
text: A man is dead, and nothing I write here changes that. Corey Ruiz was 38. His mother buried her son in August. If you’ve worn a badge long enough, you’ve stood with a family on the worst day of its life. You don’t forget it. I wore one for about 20 years, as a patrol officer, patrol sergeant, field training officer, evidence technician and hostage negotiator. Today I’m vice chair of the Assembly Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety. So let me say it plainly. The officer who shot Corey Ruiz followed the law and kept his oath to serve and protect. On Thursday, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne found no criminal liability for any Madison police officer in the July 22 officer-involved shooting. Ozanne is a Democrat in one of the most liberal counties in Wisconsin. He was appointed by Gov. Jim Doyle in 2010 and is the first Black district attorney in the state’s history. He met privately with the Ruiz family. Then he applied the law to the facts. He made the right call. Most of his fellow Democrats couldn’t bring themselves to do the same. Let’s start with the law, because the law isn’t in dispute. In 2021, Wisconsin put a statewide use-of-force standard into law. It came out of the Assembly Speaker’s Task Force on Racial Disparities. The task force’s co-chair was state Rep. Shelia Stubbs, D-Madison, and she chaired the workgroup that drafted the definition. When the bipartisan bill was signed, she said it had been an honor to lead the effort. “Now this standard is law across the state of Wisconsin,” Stubbs said . Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, signed it on Aug. 6, 2021, and praised its “clear use of force standards.” Here’s what that law says. An officer may use force that’s objectively reasonable under the totality of the circumstances. That includes three things: how serious the alleged crime is, whether the suspect poses an imminent threat to officers or others, and whether he’s actively resisting or trying to get away. Deadly force is a last resort. An officer can use it only when he reasonably believes “all other options have been exhausted or would be ineffective,” and only to stop behavior that has caused or imminently threatens death or great bodily harm. That’s the test every cop in Wisconsin is held to. Democrats helped write it. A Democratic governor signed it. Ozanne decided the criminal question under the self-defense statute, which he took the unusual step of printing in his decision. I’m going to use the tougher yardstick, the one officers are trained on and judged by. Let’s go through it. What follows comes from Ozanne’s four-page decision and from the state’s investigative file , which the Department of Justice released the same day. It’s nearly 1,800 pages of officer interviews, video reviews and evidence reports. State law requires outside investigators when an officer is involved in a death. Here, that was the Division of Criminal Investigation, which answers to Attorney General Josh Kaul. He’s a Democrat too. First, the severity of the crime. Just after 12:40 p.m., a woman called 911. She told police a man had come into her fenced backyard and she believed he tried to get into her house. The officer who took the report believed children were inside with her. She set off the alarm on her Ring camera, and he left on one of the family’s bikes. A neighborhood officer who knew Ruiz from prior professional contacts identified him from that doorbell video. Ozanne described officers trying to apprehend a man wanted for the attempted burglary of an occupied home. That’s a felony. Second, flight. The officer called for backup before attempting contact. Officers in full uniform, in marked and unmarked squads, hit their lights and sirens. One gave the command: police, stop. Ruiz rode past them, and officers lost sight of him twice. When a sergeant finally stepped onto the South Baldwin Street sidewalk with his arms out to stop him, Ruiz didn’t stop. He clipped the sergeant’s arm and went down. Third, active resistance. Ruiz ended up in the middle of the intersection at South Baldwin and Williamson streets with the sergeant on his back. He kept both arms under his body, with his hands near his waist. On the squad car audio, officers yell “Hands behind your back!” and “Quit reaching in your waist!” again and again, according to the state’s log of the recording. The officer who fired later told a supervisor the sergeant ordered Ruiz to get his hands out “at least a hundred times.” Two more officers went hands-on to get him into handcuffs. He failed to comply. Fourth, the imminent threat. With three officers on him, Ruiz pulled a knife and held it in his right hand. The officer working on that arm told investigators he felt pain, looked down and saw a silver blade with a black handle. He called it out. On the audio, officers yell “He’s got a knife!” over and over. Ruiz kept struggling and got to his feet. Wisconsin’s training manual for officers breaks an imminent threat into three parts: intent, weapon, and delivery system. The weapon was a kitchen utility knife with a 5.5-inch blade, according to the state’s evidence report. The delivery system was arm’s length, and state training puts the danger zone for an edged weapon at any distance where an officer reasonably perceives an imminent threat. As for intent, the state’s scene report says Ruiz “brandished a knife and cut a MAPD officer.” The officer who was cut is the officer who fired. Madison Police Chief John Patterson said one officer’s hands had slash marks consistent with a knife. The sergeant behind Ruiz was bleeding when it was over and went to the hospital too. Finally, the last resort. Presence had failed. Dialogue had failed. Three officers going hands-on had failed. The sergeant hit Ruiz once in the head with a closed fist. It had no effect, he told investigators, and Ruiz kept the knife. A fourth officer arrived, announced the Taser three times and deployed it. Another officer deployed a second Taser at close range. Probes struck Ruiz’s left hand and left side. He didn’t appear affected. Axon, the company that makes the Taser, examined one of them for the state. Its analysis found the two were fired within a second of each other, at such close range that the probes couldn’t spread far enough to lock up his muscles. Notice what those officers did. Madison’s own use-of-force policy says that when a subject is believed to be armed with a dangerous weapon, “an ECD is not a substitute for deadly force.” The same policy says an officer shouldn’t use a Taser on an armed subject unless another officer at the scene can deliver deadly force immediately. Cops call that lethal cover. The officer who fired told investigators he knew that rule when he heard someone yell “Taser!” State training says officers don’t have to climb the ladder one rung at a time. Policy and training didn’t require these officers to answer a knife at arm’s length with a Taser. They tried two Tasers anyway. They gave Corey Ruiz every chance the situation allowed. They warned him, too. During the struggle, an officer can be heard on the squad audio yelling, “You’re going to get shot, let go!” On police dash camera video released by the state, the knife is in Ruiz’s right hand with the blade pointed down when the Taser is deployed. The state agent who reviewed that video second by second logged it this way. At 1:34:02 p.m., an object that appeared to be an edged weapon was in Ruiz’s right hand while he was on his feet. At 1:34:03, he went down onto his right side. At 1:34:04, the officer drew his gun. The agent noted the times are approximate. The officer fired three rounds at close range. Two struck, one in the torso and one in the head. That officer told investigators he’d been on his knees fighting to control Ruiz’s right arm when he realized Ruiz had a knife. He said Ruiz’s right hand was breaking free, and he feared Ruiz would stab the sergeant, who was right behind Ruiz, in the neck or face. That’s what the statute describes: behavior that imminently threatens great bodily harm to the officer or another person. He wasn’t the only one who saw it that way. The sergeant told investigators he feared he could be stabbed and that Ruiz was within lunge distance of the officers. The officer with the first Taser said she feared Ruiz would kill or injure the officers fighting him, and she worried about the people watching. Minutes after the shooting, she told a detective that Ruiz made a stabbing motion toward one of the officers, the detective wrote. A neighbor who watched from her patio told police she saw Ruiz reaching into his waist area and heard an officer yell that he had a knife.   One more thing, and it’s in Ozanne’s own decision . Toxicology found methamphetamine in Ruiz’s system, along with two substances the body makes when it breaks down cocaine, and a presumptive positive for marijuana, and a partial glass crack pipe was inventoried at his autopsy. A bystander’s phone shows what a fight looked like from the outside. It can’t show what an officer felt in his hands or saw from his knees. Ruiz was on the ground when the shots were fired. The family’s attorney, Ben Crump, says the officer stepped back, drew and fired at point-blank range after Ruiz had been hit with a Taser. Ruiz was on the ground. That part isn’t in dispute. It’s also not the whole picture. Ruiz had been on the ground once already. That’s where he pulled the knife, under three officers, before he fought his way back to his feet. About two seconds before the officer drew, the knife was in Ruiz’s hand. Going to the ground didn’t disarm him the first time. No officer in that fight could assume it disarmed him the second time. And it hadn’t. The officer told investigators that when he grabbed Ruiz’s right wrist after the shots, Ruiz was still holding the knife. The sergeant said he moved the knife away from Ruiz. On the squad video, an officer moves it out from in front of Ruiz seconds after the shots. Two other officers saw it on the ground near his head. Then there’s the third round. Crump says the medical examiner told the family Ruiz would have survived without the shot to the head. Wisconsin’s training manual is clear: “when the threat stops, you must stop shooting.” It’s just as clear that an officer’s judgment rests on his reasonable perception of the threat in that moment. The officer told investigators he fired a third time because he didn’t think the first two rounds had hit. Nothing in Ruiz’s face or body had changed, he said. He was firing with the sergeant right behind Ruiz, worried he’d hit him. The manual gives deadly force one purpose: to stop the threat. Within a day of the shooting, state Rep. Francesca Hong, D-Madison, then a candidate for governor, told a crowd through a megaphone, “This state sanctioned violence was an execution,” as WRN reported . The state’s investigation was barely a day old. I spoke that week too. I said I believed the officer had met the legal burden, and I said my view rested on what was known then and that the district attorney would make the final call. That’s the difference between an opinion and a verdict. Four months later, the investigation is finished, and the Democrats’ statements haven’t gotten any better. Evers said he knows many Wisconsinites are angry and frustrated, and he offered his prayers to Ruiz’s family. For the officer who was cut, and for the four officers on leave, he had not one word . Gov.-elect David Crowley called the video deeply troubling and said it raises serious questions about the force used. He spoke of people who wonder whether officers are “held to the same standards as everyone else.” Ozanne had already answered that. The law applies equally to law enforcement and to everyone else, he wrote, and the self-defense statute he referred to is the same one that protects every citizen of this state. State Sen. Kelda Roys, D-Madison, called the decision another example of a system that “fails to hold the powerful to account.” State Sen. Dora Drake, D-Milwaukee, said an officer chose to shoot Ruiz at point-blank range and that his family was denied its day in court. Hong called the decision disturbing. And Stubbs, who led the effort to write the standard? She said she was shocked there’d be no charges and called the shooting “a senseless act.” Not one of those statements mentions the knife. NOT ONE. Not one mentions the officer who was cut. Not one mentions the Tasers, the commands, or the fight. They didn’t get the facts wrong. They left the facts out. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway went further. In a seven-paragraph statement that never mentions the knife either, she wrote that it’s difficult for the department to have the community’s trust “while officers involved in shootings remain on the force.” Did you catch that? Not officers who break the law, ‘Officers involved in shootings.’ She noted that only the Police and Fire Commission can discipline or fire an officer, named termination as a possible outcome and said she hopes the commission will take action. She also wrote that, as far as possible, officers should never be placed where they must make a split-second decision about force. On the squad audio, less than 30 seconds pass between officers calling out that Ruiz is on the ground and the shots. The man holding the knife took that choice away from them. Think about what this tells the officers of that department. They followed their training. They tried Tasers against a knife. One of them was cut. A Democratic prosecutor cleared them after a state investigation. And their mayor still told the city it’s hard to trust the department while they’re on it. No officer starts a shift hoping to use deadly force, and none forgets the day it was required of him. This officer had never used deadly force in more than a decade on the job. He’s a certified firearms instructor who trains other Madison officers, and he has served on the department’s SWAT team and as a mental health liaison officer. He and three other officers have spent four months on leave, enduring threats and harassment. The hostility started the first night. According to an officer’s report in the state’s file, a protester with a folding knife clipped to his jeans chased officers to a squad car and jumped in front of it to keep them from leaving. The internal review may keep these four officers on leave into next year. To the Ruiz family: You lost a son, a brother, and a father. No finding from a prosecutor makes the loss any easier. So here’s what I’m asking. Finish the internal review promptly, and publish it. A review that drags on for a year is its own kind of punishment for the officers and their families. Read the state’s report before you speak. It’s nearly 1,800 pages, and it’s public. End the threats against these officers and their families. Now. And to my Democratic colleagues: You helped write the standard. Your governor signed it. A Democratic attorney general’s investigators gathered the facts. A Democratic district attorney found no crime. Hold those facts up to your own standard, as I’ve done here. Then tell your constituents the truth. Start with the knife. The officer’s use of deadly force was completely justified, period. The men and women of the Madison Police Department already know that. They deserve leaders who will say so. Jim Piwowarczyk, R-Hubertus, represents the 98th Assembly District and is vice chair of the Assembly Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety. title: Wisconsin Fraternal Order of Police has issued a forceful statement defending the law enforcement officers involved in the deadly shooting of Corey Ruiz - Civic Media
text: Mark Sette, President of the Wisconsin Fraternal Order of Police, has issued a forceful statement defending the law enforcement officers involved in the deadly shooting of Corey Ruiz in Madison. Governor Evers offered public sympathy strictly to the family and friends of Ruiz, while Mayor Rhodes-Conway expressed concern regarding public trust when officers involved in deadly shootings remain on the force. Sette strongly rejected these assessments, arguing that political leaders failed to acknowledge the bravery of the officers or the reality that Ruiz’s own choices—resisting arrest and confronting officers with a knife after less-lethal options failed—directly caused the tragic outcome. In his statement, Sette offered firm praise and gratitude for Officers Battinger-Peterson, Vogel, Davila, and Sgt. Dabbs. He emphasized that the officers acted lawfully, professionally, and in self-defense according to independent investigations. Sette reaffirmed the Wisconsin FOP’s unwavering support for the four officers and their families as they heal and move forward in their careers, while extending appreciation to law enforcement personnel across the state.

title: Democrats’ Unlikely 2028 Senate Frontrunner - The Heartland Post
text: Francesca Hong may have lost the Democratic primary for governor, but she certainly isn’t acting like someone preparing to disappear from Wisconsin politics. Three months after coming within fewer than 4,000 votes of winning the Democratic nomination, the Madison democratic socialist remains a prominent figure in Wisconsin’s rapidly changing political landscape. Following her primary defeat, Hong launched her eight-stop “We Make Better Possible” tour across Wisconsin, continuing to organize alongside former campaign manager Becky Cooper. And while Hong initially appeared reluctant to embrace the man who defeated her, she ultimately emerged as a team player, traveling thousands of miles to campaign for David Crowley and encouraging her supporters to help Democrats secure a governing trifecta. That reconciliation could prove politically valuable. Hong’s surprisingly strong gubernatorial campaign exposed a significant ideological divide within the Democratic Party, with Gov. Tony Evers and other prominent Democrats ultimately coalescing around Crowley as Hong threatened to capture the nomination. Hong hasn’t forgotten that intervention. In a post-primary interview with Vox , she expressed disappointment with Evers’s endorsement, arguing that the governor had put his thumb on the scale and dismissed the hundreds of thousands of voters energized by her campaign. But her willingness to help elect Crowley has also given her an opportunity to build goodwill with mainstream Democrats who were hesitant to embrace her candidacy. More recently, Hong has emerged as something of a mediator between the incoming Crowley administration and the Democratic Party’s increasingly vocal socialist left who remains skeptical of how Crowley will govern. When Crowley appeared to backtrack on his commitment to Medicaid expansion , Hong quickly came to his defense, acknowledging his budgetary concerns while simultaneously arguing that Wisconsin’s surplus could cover the costs of expansion. Hey folks! So it's true that Trump's Republicans sabotaged Medicaid expansion in the "Big Beautiful Bill." A small, targeted provision in OBBBA reduces how much states that expand Medicaid can raise outside of federal funds each year, shifting the burden to public money… For now, Hong finds herself in a delicate political balancing act. As the de facto conscience of the party’s progressive wing, Hong is uniquely positioned to keep socialist activists from turning against Crowley before he even takes office. At the same time, that influence gives her a powerful platform to hold the incoming governor accountable to his campaign promises and pressure his administration to move further to the left. And with Democrats preparing to control the governor’s office and both chambers of the Legislature, Hong will have no shortage of opportunities to exercise that influence. It also gives her an opportunity to leverage her newfound political clout into another run for higher office. At just 38 years old, Hong has plenty of time to chart the next chapter of her political career. But politics is also about seizing the moment, and with her political stock still riding high following a surprisingly strong gubernatorial campaign, Hong may not want to wait too long. The question, then, may be less about whether Hong will seek higher office again and more about which office she has her sights set on. There has been plenty of speculation about what office Hong might seek next. One possibility was Madison mayor, particularly after incumbent Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would not seek another term in 2027. Hong, however, has unequivocally ruled out entering the race. The more popular theory has been that Hong will eventually challenge longtime Rep. Mark Pocan in Wisconsin’s deep-blue 2nd Congressional District. Such a campaign would fit a national trend of democratic socialist candidates challenging longtime Democratic incumbents in safe blue districts, particularly when activists believe those incumbents have become too comfortable with the party establishment. But Hong’s gubernatorial campaign demonstrated that her political appeal extends considerably further than Madison. Hong carried Dane County with roughly 44% of the vote compared with Crowley’s 37%, but she also ran nearly even with Crowley in Milwaukee County while winning Brown, Outagamie, Winnebago, Eau Claire and La Crosse counties. Statewide, she captured nearly 40% of the Democratic primary vote despite beginning the campaign as a relatively unknown Madison legislator. Her strong showing beyond Madison, coupled with her newfound statewide name recognition and established grassroots infrastructure, gives her a foundation for a potential U.S. Senate campaign in 2028. And Hong hasn’t exactly closed the door on that possibility. During a recent interview with Isthmus , Hong said she has no immediate plans to seek another office and is still processing her gubernatorial defeat. But while she emphatically ruled out running for Madison mayor, she was noticeably less definitive when asked about a potential Senate campaign. Republican Sen. Ron Johnson’s seat will be on the ballot in 2028, and the three-term incumbent has yet to announce whether he intends to seek another term. Recent reporting indicates Johnson has begun preliminary conversations with longtime campaign advisers about the possibility of running for a fourth term, although he has emphasized that no decision has been made. News: @SenRonJohnson , who once pledged to serve only 2 terms in Washington, D.C., has begun preliminary conversations with top aides about running for a 4th term in '28, according to 2 sources with knowledge of his thinking. See more in today's PM Update: https://t.co/Wqxw8wfCgx On the Republican side, Congressman Bryan Steil was widely viewed as a potential successor should Johnson retire. However, his unexpected defeat to Democrat Mitchell Berman in November has complicated that scenario. Businessman and 2024 Senate nominee Eric Hovde has indicated he could make a third Senate run, while Congressman Tony Wied and Franklin businessman Scott Mayer have also expressed interest. Democrats, meanwhile, have no shortage of familiar names who could enter the race. Former Democratic Party of Wisconsin Chairman Ben Wikler is widely discussed as a potential candidate and has raised his public profile with a statewide and national book tour, featuring stops in every major Wisconsin media market as well as liberal donor hubs like San Francisco, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. SCOOP: Ben Wikler is making moves on a 2028 Senate run, according to people who have directly spoken to him about timing and taking potential positions on his team. One source said his book tour was a dry run for a statewide campaign. me & @abedelman https://t.co/uDuWsRix1H Wikler would enter the race with a formidable fundraising network, national connections and extensive knowledge of Wisconsin’s Democratic political infrastructure. He would also face an important question: Can his success as a political operative behind the scenes translate into success as a candidate on the ballot? Wikler has never run for public office, and his close association with the Democratic establishment could present challenges among the party’s increasingly vocal socialist wing. While Wikler played a central role in rebuilding Wisconsin’s Democratic Party and helping Democrats regain control of state government, he also represents the institutional wing of the party that Hong and her supporters have frequently criticized. A longtime political insider with deep ties to wealthy donors and national Democratic leadership, Wikler represents a more traditional approach to Democratic politics built around coalition-building, fundraising and incremental gains. The contrast between Wikler and Hong would be stark. Attorney General Josh Kaul and incoming Lt. Gov. Sarah Godlewski are two other familiar statewide Democrats who could plausibly enter the race. Kaul, fresh off winning a third term as attorney general, would bring established statewide name recognition, three successful general election campaigns and the ability to run for Senate without surrendering his current office. Godlewski’s circumstances have changed even more dramatically. After serving as Secretary of State, she was elected Lieutenant Governor alongside Crowley, giving her a considerably higher-profile position and a more prominent platform within the Democratic Party. But a Senate campaign would require Godlewski to turn around almost immediately after winning statewide office and launch another campaign. It would be her fourth statewide run since 2018, potentially inviting questions about her political ambitions and motivations. Both Kaul and Godlewski have demonstrated their ability to win statewide general elections. Neither, however, has demonstrated the same kind of dedicated ideological following that Hong cultivated during her gubernatorial campaign. Kaul has never faced a Democratic primary opponent, while Godlewski’s most significant attempt to build a statewide primary coalition came during the 2022 Senate race, when she struggled to gain traction, polling at just 9% before dropping out and endorsing Mandela Barnes. Wikler, Kaul and Godlewski have different political backgrounds and strengths, but all three are closely associated with the Democratic Party’s mainstream establishment. They would likely compete for many of the same donors, activists and primary voters. Hong would enter that field from an entirely different direction. Hong would enter the Senate race with something she lacked when first entered the governor’s race: momentum. She would no longer enter a statewide primary as an obscure Madison legislator hoping to catch fire. Her political brand is established, she has developed a statewide donor network and grassroots infrastructure, and she has an opportunity over the next two years to broaden the coalition she assembled in 2026. And while Wikler, Kaul and Godlewski may be the more conventional Democratic candidates on paper, Hong’s nearly 40% showing in the gubernatorial primary gives her a distinctive starting point. If that coalition remains intact, Hong would begin a Senate campaign with an established base of support while her potential rivals compete for much of the remaining electorate. While some of Hong’s supporters could certainly defect to other candidates, her political floor appears remarkably high. She has cultivated an intensely loyal following, and barring another progressive challenger competing for the same ideological base, it’s difficult to envision a significant portion of that coalition abandoning her in 2028. And there is little reason to assume that 40% represents her political ceiling. Hong would have another two years to build on the momentum of her gubernatorial campaign, expand her fundraising network and introduce herself to voters who may have overlooked her the first time around. Much will depend on whether the socialist movement’s recent political momentum continues into 2028. With prominent progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ro Khanna both discussed as potential presidential candidates, the next Democratic presidential primary could provide a national platform for the same ideological movement that powered Hong’s gubernatorial campaign. The direction of the Crowley administration could also shape the political environment. If Crowley successfully unites the party’s competing factions and delivers on the progressive priorities that helped Democrats win their trifecta, some of the urgency behind Hong’s insurgent movement could fade. If ideological tensions persist, however, the divide exposed during the gubernatorial primary could become an even more important feature of the next statewide Democratic primary. If Crowley delivers on the progressive priorities that helped Democrats win their trifecta, Hong could claim some of the credit for championing those reforms while making the case for taking that agenda to Washington. If Crowley falls short of her expectations, however, it could just as easily strengthen her argument against the party’s more corporatist establishment and reinforce her case for why Democrats need a democratic socialist representing them in the U.S. Senate. A similar ideological struggle is already playing out in Washington, where the progressive wing of the new Democratic Senate majority has rallied behind Chris Van Hollen for majority leader over the more establishment-backed Chuck Schumer. That divide could provide Hong with another opportunity to frame a potential Senate campaign as part of a broader movement to reshape the Democratic Party from within. Hong has no shortage of options before her, and plenty could change between now and 2028. She could take the potentially safer route of challenging Mark Pocan in Wisconsin’s deep-blue 2nd Congressional District. She could forgo another campaign altogether, maintaining her position as a prominent organizer and influential voice within the Democratic Party’s progressive wing. Or she could set her sights on something bigger. And if Hong decides to make a run for the U.S. Senate, she could find herself in an unfamiliar position: no longer the insurgent underdog, but the candidate her Democratic rivals would have to beat.

title: Wisconsin Fraternal Order of Police has issued a forceful statement defending the law enforcement officers involved in the deadly shooting of Corey Ruiz - Civic Media
text: Mark Sette, President of the Wisconsin Fraternal Order of Police, has issued a forceful statement defending the law enforcement officers involved in the deadly shooting of Corey Ruiz in Madison. Pushing back against comments from Governor Tony Evers and Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, Sette highlighted the severe risks and emotional toll faced by officers in the line of duty while offering firm support for those involved. Governor Evers offered public sympathy strictly to the family and friends of Ruiz, while Mayor Rhodes-Conway expressed concern regarding public trust when officers involved in deadly shootings remain on the force. Sette strongly rejected these assessments, arguing that political leaders failed to acknowledge the bravery of the officers or the reality that Ruiz’s own choices—resisting arrest and confronting officers with a knife after less-lethal options failed—directly caused the tragic outcome. In his statement, Sette offered firm praise and gratitude for Officers Battinger-Peterson, Vogel, Davila, and Sgt. Dabbs. He emphasized that the officers acted lawfully, professionally, and in self-defense according to independent investigations. Sette reaffirmed the Wisconsin FOP’s unwavering support for the four officers and their families as they heal and move forward in their careers, while extending appreciation to law enforcement personnel across the state.
